articles.title: Newcastle photographer's Matty Healy photo shortlisted for award
articles.summary: Neil Ferry is shortlisted for a British Photography Award for his snap of Matty Healy.
articles.body:
A photographer has been shortlisted for a national award for a portrait he took of Matty Healy.

Neil Ferry, 56, from Newcastle, took the photo in just a couple of minutes while the 1975 frontman was rehearsing for his Sunday for Sammy performance in February.

Ferry said Healy, 37, was a "lovely guy" and more than willing to give his time.

The snap is just one of three photos Ferry is shortlisted for at this year's British Photography Awards, with the winners announced on 1 November.

Sunday for Sammy, which features a host of well-known TV, theatre and music stars from the north-east of England, began in 2000 in honour of actor Sammy Johnson, known for his roles in Auf Wiedersehen, Pet and Spender, who died in 1998.

The musician's dad, actor Tim Healy, was one of the show's founders.

Ferry only started taking photos at aged 48, eventually deciding to do a BA at Newcastle College.

Although it is now his great passion, he makes his living selling pianos.

Through his work photographing musicians in Newcastle, Ferry's friend who runs Beyond Vinyl, told him Healy was there rehearsing and to come and ask him for a photo.

"So I went in, he was really busy, lovely, lovely guy and he said 'look, you know, I'm rehearsing, but I've got a couple of minutes before I go home,'" Ferry said.

"I literally only had a minute to do the photo."

His friend sat in as the test subject while Ferry got everything set up for the photo shoot.

"[Healy] was really tired because he'd been obviously rehearsing all day, but that really made the photograph, in my opinion," the photographer said.

"And I loved the fact that he was a bit weary, I just think it really makes the photo."

Ferry has another photograph shortlisted in the portrait category of another musician, Nick Celino.

He is up against photographers from around the country whose photos feature the likes of Ncuti Gatwa and trainspotting influencer Francis Bourgeois.

Ferry has another shortlisted in the Wedding category.

articles.title: Greve de alunos do ensino médio na França ganha apoio de universidades | G1
articles.standfirst: Estudantes do ensino médio reivindicam principalmente a substituição de professores ausentes e mais recursos para a educação. A situação atingiu o ápice a poucos dias da apresentação do orçamento e a poucos meses de uma eleição presidencial na qual a extrema direita aparece como favorita.
articles.summary: Estudantes do ensino médio reivindicam principalmente a substituição de professores ausentes e mais recursos para a educação. País está a poucos meses de uma eleição presidencial.
articles.body:
Alunos universitários e de ensino médio protestam na França. — Foto: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

Cerca de 30 universidades aderiram nesta quinta-feira (1º) ao movimento de bloqueio de escolas de ensino médio que se espalha pela França, ampliando uma mobilização iniciada há cerca de uma semana. Segundo a União Estudantil, campi estão bloqueados em Paris, Estrasburgo, Marselha, Lyon, Reims, Poitiers e Nanterre, entre outras cidades. O sindicato classificou a adesão como “histórica”. Os acessos estão impedidos, mas as universidades podem manter as aulas à distância.

Os estudantes do ensino médio reivindicam principalmente a substituição de professores ausentes e mais recursos para a educação. A adesão dos universitários é apresentada pelos sindicatos estudantis como o “ato dois” da mobilização, que ganhou força nos últimos dias e foi marcada também por episódios de violência.

O movimento atingiu 356 escolas na quarta-feira (30), contra 338 na terça, segundo o Ministério do Interior. Naquele dia, 625 pessoas foram detidas e 83 policiais e gendarmes ficaram feridos. Desde o início dos bloqueios, 119 estudantes e funcionários de escolas foram feridos, segundo o balanço divulgado pelo ministro da Educação francês, Édouard Geffray.

Nesta quinta-feira, os bloqueios continuavam em Paris, Marselha (sul), Estrasburgo (leste) e Rennes (noroeste).

“Eles não nos escutam, somos obrigados a sair às ruas” , disse à AFP Lola, estudante do segundo ano do ensino médio. Ela citou jornadas de 8h às 18h, professores que não são substituídos e turmas sem professor responsável entre os motivos da mobilização.

Em Estrasburgo, cerca de 500 quilômetros a leste de Paris, centenas de estudantes, muitos vestidos de preto, bloquearam a circulação diante da escola Couffignal, inclusive o tráfego de bondes. Grandes contêineres de lixo foram colocados no chão e incendiados.

Aumento da tensão social, greve e protesto estudantil

Neste semana, a França enfrenta uma onda de protestos, com greve de servidores públicos e confrontos entre estudantes e policiais. A situação atingiu o ápice a poucos dias da apresentação do orçamento e a poucos meses de uma eleição presidencial na qual a extrema direita aparece como favorita.

Na terça-feira (29), cerca de 200 mil manifestantes foram às ruas em todo o país, dos quais quase 30 mil em Paris, segundo o Ministério do Interior. Mais de 170 marchas foram convocadas para reivindicar reajustes dos salários dos servidores, corroídos pela inflação, e "recursos orçamentários à altura" das necessidades da administração pública.

"Mesmo com 40°C, nossos salários continuam congelados" , dizia um cartaz na marcha em Lyon, após um verão de calor intenso que pôs à prova os bombeiros e o sistema de saúde.

"Estamos nos manifestando hoje porque precisamos ser recebidos pelo ministro", disse Nicolas March, bombeiro de 52 anos que chegou com seus colegas à Praça da Bastilha, em Paris, sob os aplausos dos demais manifestantes.

As reivindicações dos servidores incluem a perda do poder de compra, o número insuficiente de funcionários, a deterioração das condições de trabalho e, em alguns casos, a precariedade diante dos cortes orçamentários.

Manifestações de alunos de ensino médio na França. — Foto: Noemie Olive/Reuters

Estudantes do ensino médio, que protestam desde a semana passada por melhores condições na educação, protagonizaram um dia de confrontos violentos na terça-feira. Grupos de adolescentes incendiaram contêineres de lixo e lançaram objetos contra a polícia, que respondeu com golpes de cassetetes e bombas de gás lacrimogêneo.

Os conflitos levaram à detenção de 440 pessoas , informou o Ministério do Interior. Também houve feridos, entre eles dez funcionários e vários alunos.

O ministro da Educação, Édouard Geffray, anunciou a abertura de ações judiciais pelos atos de violência.

"Essa violência é indescritível (...) Legitimá-la ou pedir, neste contexto, que os bloqueios sejam ampliados é colocar em perigo tanto nossos alunos quanto os servidores públicos", escreveu na rede X.

Os estudantes mantinham bloqueios e protestos em centenas de escolas de ensino médio pelo país. Suas queixas abrangiam a organização dos horários, o tamanho das turmas, a falta de professores e as salas de aula superaquecidas durante as recentes ondas de calor.

Alunos da França fazem protestos com foto em Saint-Denis, próximo a Paris. — Foto: Abdul Saboor/Reuters

Alguns episódios de violência registrados durante os bloqueios levaram à abertura de três investigações pela IGPN, órgão que investiga a atuação da polícia. Segundo o ministro do Interior, Laurent Nuñez, as investigações dizem respeito a incidentes ocorridos em Sevran, na região parisiense, Saint-Ouen-l'Aumône, no Val-d'Oise, norte de Paris, e na cidade de Tours, no centro-oeste da França.

Em Tours, um estudante ficou ferido na cabeça na quarta-feira e foi hospitalizado. Segundo o Ministério Público, suas lesões são “compatíveis” com um disparo de armas utilizadas pelas forças de segurança francesas para conter manifestações.

As autoridades também registraram, em diferentes cidades, incêndios de lixeiras, disparos de morteiros e construção de barricadas, além de detenções relacionadas aos protestos . Nuñez afirmou que as forças de segurança intervieram “com muita proporcionalidade”.

O presidente da União Sindical dos Estudantes de Ensino Médio (USL), Ryad Rani, e a secretária-geral da União Estudantil, Eloïse Lefebvre-Milon, convocaram uma ampliação da mobilização para esta quinta-feira e para terça-feira, 6 de outubro. As organizações pedem, entre outras medidas, um “financiamento maciço dos liceus e das universidades”.

A Unef, terceira maior organização estudantil, também convocou universitários a sair às ruas em todo o país. Entre suas reivindicações estão a oposição à redução do número de vagas nas universidades e ao congelamento dos auxílios habitacionais.

Diante da expansão dos protestos, o governo anunciou na quarta-feira a criação de uma “plataforma de consulta” aberta a todos os estudantes do ensino médio. Eles poderão apresentar suas reivindicações e preocupações de forma regionalizada. Segundo Geffray, uma “restituição nacional” será posteriormente organizada para apresentar “respostas estruturadas”.

articles.title: Ônibus perde o freio e atinge veículos em Santa Cruz do Rio Pardo | G1
articles.standfirst: Coletivo passava por manutenção elétrica e estava estacionado em frente a uma oficina no momento do incidente, na tarde desta terça-feira (29). Ninguém ficou ferido.
articles.summary: Um ônibus que passava por manutenção elétrica perdeu o freio e atingiu dois veículos em Santa Cruz do Rio Pardo; o incidente não deixou feridos.
articles.body:
Um ônibus perdeu o freio, atingiu dois veículos e parou de ré em uma rua de Santa Cruz do Rio Pardo (SP), nesta terça-feira (29).

O coletivo passava por manutenção na parte elétrica e o incidente aconteceu quando o motorista estava dentro do veículo, que se encontrava estacionado em frente à oficina mecânica.

Ônibus perde o freio, atinge dois veículos e para de ré em rua de Santa Cruz do Rio Pardo — Foto: Câmera de Segurança

Imagens de câmeras de segurança registraram o momento em que o ônibus perde o freio e passa a descer a rua de ré. Durante o percurso, o coletivo atinge um caminhão que estava estacionado na via.

Na sequência da gravação, é possível ver que o veículo continua descendo de ré até bater em um carro de passeio. Após o impacto, o ônibus cruza a rua e para.

Segundo testemunhas, o coletivo havia sido levado ao local para reparos na parte elétrica. Apesar do susto e dos danos materiais nos veículos atingidos, ninguém ficou ferido.

O g1 tenta contato com a rede de postos Graal, cuja marca estampa o coletivo, mas não obteve retorno até a última atualização desta reportagem.

articles.title: Brenda Bulhões: mãe fecha salão onde filha foi morta dois anos depois | G1
articles.standfirst: Elisangela da Silva manteve o negócio por quase dois anos após o assassinato da filha, em Guarujá (SP). Brenda foi morta ao chegar para trabalhar em 2024.
articles.summary: Elisangela da Silva fez de tudo para manter vivo o sonho da filha, mas não consegue mais sustentar o comércio em Guarujá (SP). Brenda Bulhões foi morta ao chegar para trabalhar.
articles.body:
A cabeleireira Elisangela da Silva decidiu fechar o salão de beleza onde trabalhava com a filha, a empresária Brenda Bulhões , executada a tiros em frente ao estabelecimento em Guarujá , no litoral de São Paulo. Ao g1 , ela contou que tentou manter o negócio por quase dois anos para preservar o sonho da filha, mas não conseguiu mais sustentar o espaço.

"Sempre foi o sonho da Brenda. Foi mais dela do que meu. Eu sinto que falhei, mas sozinha não consigo. Se os clientes não vão, eu não consigo. Ali a gente tem tudo o que ela sempre sonhou, é tudo do jeito dela e destruir aquilo de alguma forma me dói, me enfraquece", lamentou Elisangela.

Brenda foi baleada quando chegava para trabalhar no salão, no bairro Paecará, em 29 de novembro de 2024 ( assista acima ). O ex-companheiro dela, Bruno dos Santos Campos , é apontado como o principal suspeito do crime e foi preso dois meses depois, na fronteira do Brasil com o Paraguai.

Brenda Bulhões foi morta na porta do salão de beleza que mantinha com a mãe em Guarujá — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

Elisangela retomou o trabalho no salão no mês seguinte ao assassinato. Segundo ela, a decisão foi uma forma de honrar o compromisso da filha com os clientes, principalmente por causa da proximidade das festas de fim de ano. "Eu sabia que não teria vaga em outros salões", afirmou.

No entanto, o retorno ao local do crime foi extremamente difícil para a cabeleireira. "No primeiro dia, eu não conseguia nem abrir [o salão]. Eu tive a ajuda dos vizinhos", afirmou.

Ainda segundo Elisangela, ela precisou do incentivo da família para tocar o negócio, que era administrado por Brenda. " Voltei porque o meu marido insistiu muito, disse que era o sonho dela ", explicou.

A cabeleireira enfrentou outras dificuldades. Ela não conhecia muitos dos clientes atendidos por Brenda e precisou restringir os horários de funcionamento para cuidar da neta deixada pela filha.

Elisangela contou que viu o estabelecimento esvaziar aos poucos e passou a sofrer muito com a situação. Ela chegou a buscar alternativas, inclusive contratando outras profissionais, mas não conseguiu reverter o cenário.

Brenda Bulhões era cabeleireira em Guarujá — Foto: Redes sociais

"Eu fiquei lutando até que eu vi que não ia conseguir mais. Eu lutei de tudo quanto é forma", lamentou.

Apesar do fechamento, Elisangela afirmou que pretende continuar trabalhando como cabeleireira, inclusive com atendimentos domiciliares.

"Todo mundo diz que são ciclos que se fecham para abrir outro, mas ainda não consigo ver dessa forma. Estou bem triste, mas é porque eu passei um ano e dez meses lutando ali, com dor, sem dor, tinha hora que eu não conseguia nem respirar. Depois a gente vai até se acostumando, mas é com muita tristeza que eu fecho esse salão", afirmou.

Elisangela da Silva é mãe de Brenda Bulhões, morta a tiros em Guarujá (SP) — Foto: Reprodução/TV Tribuna

Mãe, filha, irmã, amiga e empreendedora do ramo de beleza, Brenda Bulhões deixou uma filha que, na época, tinha 9 anos.

A empresária morreu dias antes de completar 27 anos. Ela nasceu na mesma data do irmão dela, mas sete anos depois. Por isso, a dupla costumava celebrar junto os aniversários. Em 2024, a mãe dela contou que Brenda mantinha os preparativos para uma festa.

"Era aquela pessoa que se estivesse feliz, ela estava feliz demais. Se ela estivesse amando, estava amando demais. Se estivesse triste e brava, também era demais", disse a mãe dela. A cabeleireira ainda falou que desde o nascimento da neta, Brenda lutou pela filha. “Criou [a menina] e trabalhava muito para dar tudo. Tudo não é só dinheiro, mas amor”, explicou.

Brenda Bulhões (à esq.) foi morta a tiros em frente ao próprio salão de beleza em Guarujá (SP) — Foto: Redes Sociais e Reprodução

Brenda foi assassinada na Rua Pará, no bairro Paecará, por volta das 8h20 de 29 de novembro de 2024.

Imagens registraram o momento em que ela estacionou uma motocicleta em frente ao salão. Instantes depois, um homem usando capacete caminhou em direção à empresária, atirou e fugiu. A ação durou menos de um minuto.

De acordo com a prefeitura, o Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) foi acionado e realizou manobras de reanimação cardiopulmonar, mas Brenda não resistiu. A morte foi constatada no local.

articles.title: Moradora grava invasão de enxame de abelhas no quintal de casa  | G1
articles.standfirst: Ninguém se feriu no incidente, mas a moradora de Sorocaba (SP) precisou de atendimento médico após ataque de pânico.
articles.summary: Uma moradora de Sorocaba (SP) gravou o momento em que um enxame de abelhas invadiu o quintal da casa dela, no Jardim Brasilândia, na quarta-feira (30).
articles.body:
Uma moradora de Sorocaba (SP) gravou o momento em que um enxame de abelhas invadiu o quintal da casa dela, no Jardim Brasilândia, na quarta-feira (30). Ninguém se feriu, mas a mulher precisou de atendimento dos bombeiros após ter um ataque de pânico. Assista acima .

A auxiliar de educação Edvana Almeida, de 49 anos, relatou ao g1 que o quintal foi invadido por centenas de insetos enquanto o marido estava trabalhando. Ela e a cachorra de estimação da família ficaram "encurraladas" no imóvel.

Em um vídeo gravado no momento do ocorrido, Edvana conta que passou por uma situação aterrorizante, pois estava sozinha quando viu a "nuvem" de abelhas.

"Passei por uma situação bem tensa. Pela manhã, havia algumas abelhas no meu quintal, aproximadamente umas 20 ou 30, e elas estavam bem alvoroçadas. Aí, corri para trancar a minha casa porque sou alérgica", disse.

Moradora de Sorocaba gravou o momento em que um enxame de abelhas invadiu o quintal da casa dela, no Jardim Brasilândia — Foto: Arquivo pessoal

A mulher acionou o Corpo de Bombeiros e explicou que uma atendente a acalmou até a chegada da equipe de resgate. Quando os militares chegaram, a maioria das abelhas já havia ido embora.

Edvana passará por um procedimento cirúrgico nesta quinta-feira (1º), que não tem relação com o episódio. Ela está internada, mas segue acompanhando o imóvel por câmeras de segurança.

"O bombeiro explicou que são abelhas transitórias e que as que ficaram é porque estão perdidas. Pediu para evitar acender a luz ontem (quarta-feira) e que todas devem ir embora hoje (quinta-feira). Estou monitorando pela câmera de segurança e ainda tem abelhas lá", concluiu.

articles.title: Orçamento do RJ 2027: Governo prevê déficit de R$ 13,9 bilhões | G1
articles.standfirst: Proposta enviada à Alerj prevê R$ 138,3 bilhões em despesas e R$ 124,3 bilhões em receitas para o próximo ano. A gestão de Ricardo Couto prevê reduzir o rombo para R$ 2,1 bilhões com novas medidas.
articles.summary: O orçamento do RJ para 2027 prevê déficit de R$ 13,9 bilhões, mas a gestão de Ricardo Couto busca reduzir o rombo através de novas medidas fiscais.
articles.body:
O desembargador Ricardo Couto, presidente do TJ-RJ e governador em exercício do Rio — Foto: Divulgação

O governo do Rio de Janeiro enviou à Assembleia Legislativa (Alerj), nesta quarta-feira (30), a proposta de Lei Orçamentária Anual (LOA) de 2027 , que estima as receitas e fixa as despesas do estado para o próximo ano.

A proposta prevê R$ 138,3 bilhões em despesas e R$ 124,3 bilhões em receitas, o que resulta em um déficit estimado de R$ 13,9 bilhões . O valor é menor que os R$ 18,9 bilhões projetados para 2026, mas ainda representa um desafio para as contas do estado.

A Alerj tem até o fim do ano para votar o projeto. Até a votação final, os deputados ainda podem apresentar emendas e sugestões de alteração no texto.

Apesar disso, o governo trabalha com uma previsão mais otimista e estima um déficit de R$ 2,1 bilhões. A equipe econômica do governador em exercício, Ricardo Couto, calcula um acréscimo de R$ 11,8 bilhões no caixa a partir de medidas que ainda dependem de aprovação.

Entre elas estão projetos de lei já enviados à Alerj para combater a sonegação e permitir a negociação de dívidas de empresas com o estado. O governo também prevê a negociação de dívidas bancárias do estado que não estão incluídas no Programa de Pleno Pagamento de Dívidas dos Estados (Propag).

articles.title: Trump diz que está acompanhando 'muito de perto' as eleições do Brasil | G1
articles.standfirst: Presidente norte-americano também afirmou que pleito brasileiro é "muito importante". Ele não mencionou nenhum candidato. Congressistas dos EUA apontaram tentativa de interferência do governo Trump nas eleições do Brasil.
articles.summary: O presidente dosEUA, Donald Trump, afirmou que está acompanhando "muito de perto" as eleições no Brasil. Ele disse ainda que o pleito brasileiro é "muito importante".
articles.body:
Trump fala com a imprensa na Casa Branca antes de embarcar — Foto: Evan Vucci/Reuters

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, afirmou nesta quinta-feira (1º) que está acompanhando "muito de perto" as eleições no Brasil. Ele disse ainda que o pleito brasileiro é "muito importante".

"O Brasil é um país muito importante. É um ótimo país. As pessoas do Brasil são fantásticas. É uma eleição muito importante", declarou o presidente a repórteres na Casa Branca.

Trump não mencionou se está apoiando algum candidato no pleito brasileiro , rompendo com a postura que tem adotado em eleições na América Latina. No exemplo mais recente, no pleito da Colômbia, o norte-americano manifestou abertamente apoio ao agora presidente do país, Abelardo de la Espriella .

Na semana passada, congressistas norte-americanos acusaram o governo de Donald Trump de tentar interferir nas eleições brasileiras , em uma carta enviada ao secretário de Estado dos EUA, Marco Rubio. Esta semana, senadores cobraram da gestão Trump , também por meio de uma carta a Rubio, garantias de que Washington aceitará o resultado do pleito .

No novo documento, os senadores expressaram " preocupação com ações do governo (dos EUA) que ameaçam nossa aliança estratégica com o Brasil" e voltaram a apontar uma suposta tentativa de interferência por parte de Washington.

"Ao longo do segundo mandato do Presidente Trump, observamos autoridades dos EUA envolvidas em uma campanha de interferência e desestabilização no Brasil", diz o documento.

Na carta, eles apresentam, como indícios:

A nomeação de Darren Beattie, político de extrema direita e forte crítico do governo de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, como assessor sênior para questões relacionadas ao Brasil no Departamento de Estado dos EUA;

A aplicação de novas tarifas extras após uma investigação, segundo relatos, "iniciada por determinação do presidente Trump".

👉 Em agosto, o Departamento do Estado dos EUA afirmou ao g1 que respeitará "qualquer governo" que for eleito em outubro no Brasil . O departamento também negou ter um plano para impedir uma reeleição do presidente Lula .

Ainda assim, o governo brasileiro construiu uma "barreira" para tentar blindar qualquer tentativa de interferência por parte do governo Trump, de acordo com uma reportagem do jornal norte-americano "The New York Times" com base em fontes de Brasília.

Como exemplo, o Brasil tem buscado apoio de países na Europa e Ásia e monitorado lobbies estrangeiros dentro do país, além de tentar combater informações falsas sobre fraude eleitoral.

Abin informou europeus de interferência, diz agência

Flávio Bolsonaro, Donald Trump e Lula — Foto: Montagem - Arte/g1

Uma reportagem da agência de notícias Reuters afirmou que a Agência Brasileira de Inteligência (Abin) informou à União Europeia que Estados Unidos e Rússia tentaram interferir no pleito brasileiro .

Com base também em fontes e documentos da UE, a Reuters afirmou que o alerta foi feito pela Abin a delegações da Alemanha e da França que visitaram em setembro a capital brasileira. Na ocasião, afirmou a agência, autoridades da Abin “confirmaram a existência de interferência tanto dos Estados Unidos quanto da Rússia" .

Por parte do governo norte-americano, a suposta interferência veio por meio de "ações judiciais até interferência abertamente reconhecida", segundo um relatório da UE sobre a reunião ao que a Reuters teve acesso. O documento não detalhou a suposta interferência do governo da Rússia.

articles.title: UK PM Burnham says Iran likely behind RAF base incident: Is there evidence?
articles.summary: UK, US and Israeli officials point to Iranian involvement but remain tight-lipped on details.
articles.body:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK’s security services have “strong indications” of Iranian involvement in the incident at a British Royal Air Force (RAF) station near Fairford this week in which five men were arrested before they were released on bail.

The five British men were spotted near the airbase and arrested on Sunday on suspicion of “terrorism” and explosives offences, before they were released.

The United States has used the British base to carry out operations in various conflicts, including to deploy bombers in its war against Iran.

Iran has strongly denied any involvement with the airbase incident, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying British authorities are “barking up the wrong tree”.

So, what do we know about the incident, and is there evidence Iran played a role?

Authorities were alerted to suspicious activity near the base early Sunday morning, including three vans parked oddly and a group of hooded, masked men.

Police responded and arrested five British men in their early 20s in the nearby Whelford area, saying they were suspected of explosives offences. Counter Terrorism police later took over the probe and said the men were suspected of preparing “a terrorist act”.

The suspects were released on bail Monday , but remain subject to “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others,” according to the United Kingdom’s head of counter terrorism policing, Laurence Taylor.

On Tuesday, after three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said they had found no explosives in the vehicles that were parked the near the base, but had retrieved a “quantity of petrol”.

Who is linking the incident to Iran, and have they cited evidence?

Officials in the UK, the US and Israel have all pointed to Iran but offered no details.

Burnham on Wednesday spoke of “strong indications” of Iran’s involvement and said an “ongoing, complex and serious police investigation” is continuing.

However, the prime minister did not give any details on what the suspects were planning or why the UK thinks Iran was involved, saying only that he would “update people more in due course”.

In the US, President Donald Trump said the case “might be” Iran-linked and that the US had been keeping tabs on the suspects “for a long time”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the case “clearly involved the hands of a foreign actor”, without naming a specific state.

In Israel, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had forewarned the UK about a potential “Iranian-sponsored attack”.

In a statement on Monday, Iran’s embassy in London said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” any attempts to link Iran to the individuals arrested near the airbase.

It said the spread of such “fabricated speculations” fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” and that Iran reserves the right to “take appropriate legal measures”.

On Wednesday, Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said the UK was “barking up the wrong tree” by pointing to potential Iranian involvement.

Why has the UK released the suspects on bail?

It is unclear. Under British “counterterrorism law”, police can hold suspects for up to two weeks before charging them. However, if authorities find little evidence to support their initial suspicion of “terrorism”, they would have far less time – usually 24 to 36 hours, said Chris Phillips, a former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office.

“If it’s not an actual terrorist attack, then the police don’t have anywhere near as long to keep them in custody,” said Phillips. “I think the police just need more time to do their enquiries.”

Andrew Silke, professor of criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London, said the suspects could have also been released on bail while under suspicion of “terrorism” if “authorities feel relatively confident that these individuals do not pose an imminent danger of either carrying out or organising a terrorist attack”, such as if they had “peripheral” or “unknowing involvement”.

Afzal Ashraf, a visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior Royal Air Force officer, said the bail release does not necessarily indicate that the “Iranian-involvement hypothesis has been rejected” but it does mean “police have judged that these individuals did not present any immediate danger”.

Taylor, the head of counter terrorism policing, said the men’s release on bail was an “investigative decision” based on “experience and careful considerations of policing powers.” He stressed that the men are bound by “stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others” as the investigation into them continues.

But their release drew backlash in the US from Trump, who said British authorities “should not have done that”.

“How do you give bail to a terrorist?” Trump asked.

Iran’s Araghchi appeared to suggest that the suspects’ release supported Iran’s position that it was not involved.

“I can confirm Iran’s belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all,” wrote Araghchi in a post on X.

What questions about the case are still unanswered?

Questions remain about the circumstances in which authorities were initially alerted to suspicious activity near the base, the extent to which they believe the suspects are linked to Iran and what the suspects may have been planning.

According to the BBC, police received two early-morning calls on Sunday regarding suspicious vehicles near the base, the first of which the media understands was made by one of the suspects themselves.

The Times of London reported that police are looking into the suspect’s motives for making such a call, including “whether he got cold feet or whether it was part of the plan”.

Authorities are also probing whether the incident was a form of “surveillance, a ‘dry run’ to test security or a stunt to send a message to the British government”, reported The Times.

Meanwhile, police have suggested they are looking into whether the suspects could have been unwittingly acting on Iran’s behalf.

In an updated briefing on Tuesday, Taylor said officials were examining whether the activity could have been “committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.

He also spoke more generally about the “increasing breadth and complexity” of threats facing the UK, saying threats often emerge first as small-scale criminal activity, “committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain”.

Phillips told Al Jazeera he believes the suspects could have been recruited online to carry out some type of malicious activity that falls short of a “terrorist attack”.

“It sounds as though these people have been paid online to do some naughty work”, such as “setting fire to something”, said Phillips.

He said both Russia and Iran have allegedly paid “stooges” to carry out such acts in recent years. “At first glance now, it seems that that may be the case, but time will tell,” Phillips added.

Royal Holloway’s Silke also said he believes the evidence suggests “a proxy explanation”.

“Certainly, there have been recent cases in Europe where individuals have been used unwittingly as proxies by foreign governments to carry out activities which have a hostile intent,” he said. “The UK authorities in this case may have assessed that something similar had happened here, and that the individuals involved had no inherent terrorist motivation themselves, but had been caught up unintentionally in a larger plot.”

Has Iran previously been accused of plots in the UK?

Yes. MI5 Director General Ken McCallum said in October 2025 that the agency had tracked “more than 20 potentially lethal Iran-backed plots” in the UK within a year.

McCallum alleged that Iran, along with Russia, has resorted to “ugly methods,” such as “surveillance, sabotage, arson or physical violence”.

British Security Minister Dan Jarvis has said Iran often uses criminal proxies to “obfuscate” its involvement in attacks, which have targeted Iranian dissidents and Jewish and Israeli people in the country.

In March this year, British police arrested four people on suspicion of helping Iran spy on the local Jewish community. The month after, police said they were probing possible Iran links to a series of arson attacks on Jewish targets ‌in London.

In June, two Romanian men whom British prosecutors said had acted as proxies for Iran’s government were handed lengthy jail terms for stabbing a British journalist of Iranian origin who wrote for an Iranian media outlet critical of Iran’s government.

Iran’s government has repeatedly denied involvement in any illegal plots or attacks on British.

articles.title: 'The Girls' podcast debuts as co-hosts take on Lindsay Clancy case, Ms Rachel's political activism
articles.summary: Samantha Ponder's fiery take on the Lindsay Clancy case and a heated Ms. Rachel debate drive the premiere episode of "the Girls" podcast series.
articles.body: The debut episode of FOX News Podcasts’ "the Girls" delivered an unfiltered conversation where no subject was off-limits, as the hosts discussed the Lindsay Clancy trial, Ms. Rachel's political activism, the realities of grief and more. Each episode features a rotating cast of women with distinctive voices and experiences spanning news, politics, sports, comedy and culture. Thursday’s premiere brought together Fox News’ Harris Faulkner, Rachel Campos-Duffy and Kat Timpf, former secretary to New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo Melissa DeRosa and former ESPN host Samantha Ponder. The conversation got intense as Ponder weighed in on Clancy, the Massachusetts woman charged with murdering her three young children, whose trial ended in a mistrial last month. FOX NEWS MEDIA EXPANDS PODCAST PORTFOLIO WITH NEW ORIGINAL SHOW ‘THE GIRLS’ "If I’m a mom and this has been done to my kids, I want this woman put away forever," Ponder says in a preview clip. "You can say things were hard, [but] you still gotta be in prison." The group also debated whether children’s entertainer Ms. Rachel is a bad influence because of her political activism, with Timpf defending her and Faulkner questioning how much parents should know about the political views of children's entertainers. "Is Ms. Rachel bad for kids? I don't think it's that deep," Timpf said. "She just sings songs... I still listen to Michael Jackson. Where do you draw the line? I grew up listening to Nirvana. I love Kurt Cobain. I wore flannel. I've yet to shoot up heroin," she added. Faulkner said that parents should consider the political views children may absorb from online personalities. "When she says she wants to do away with ICE, when she says that she’s more for letting those people come across our border illegally, when she says those things — why do I know that about her?" Faulkner said. MOMS FOR LIBERTY CO-FOUNDER WARNS PARENTS ABOUT MS RACHEL’S POLITICAL ACTIVISM, ‘NOT MR ROGERS’ The premiere also took a more personal turn when Timpf opened up about losing her father shortly before becoming pregnant with her second child. "Not to make it weird, but I think about death pretty much all the time because my dad died," Timpf said. Timpf said she had spoken to her father the morning he died and later learned from a doctor she had never met that he had suffered an aortic dissection after initially going to the hospital with a stomach ache. Her father had been intensely focused on his health, which made his sudden death especially difficult for her to process. "He was very fit. He would not drink out of a plastic water bottle," Timpf said. "When he died, he was going up north for a day of sailing." SAM PONDER CALLS OUT THE WNBA FOR COWARDICE: 'BE COURAGEOUS. STAND FOR WOMEN' Timpf said the loss left her questioning whether people have any real control over their health or fate. She noted that her mother also died before turning 60 and that she battled cancer during her first pregnancy. "I almost learned the wrong lesson of like, ‘What can you do?’" she said. "Do I want to live forever? I’m scared so much to die." The conversations capture the podcast's freewheeling nature, covering an array of topics across news, politics, sports, comedy and culture. "the Girls'" is available on Fox News Digital, Apple, Spotify, YouTube and wherever you get your podcasts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russian dissident Garry Kasparov says US warned him of danger to his life
articles.summary: "My family and I will not truly be safe as long as Putin is in power," says the former chess world champion.
articles.body:
An exiled Russian opposition figure living in the US says he was warned by American and Lithuanian security services that his life was in danger.

Former chess world champion Garry Kasparov said he was one of two dissidents told to take precautions, which he had done.

His comments come after the US Justice Department unsealed an indictment earlier this month charging five people who allegedly work for a network linked to the Kremlin with plotting attacks and murders in countries including the US, focusing on Russian dissidents and defectors.

Kasparov wrote in his publication The Next Move that he had not been told explicitly that he and fellow Free Russia Forum co-founder Ivan Tyutrin were considered targets, but said both had been warned about their safety.

Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that it had obtained information that Kasparov, along with another Russian opposition figure, Ilya Ponomarev, had been warned about the plot over the summer by US authorities.

Citing sources close to Kasparov, the paper said he had been placed under enhanced protection over the summer for the first time since he moved to the US.

Kasparov wrote separately: "I will not stop and I will not hide, even if I thought it was possible to do so.

"My family and I will not truly be safe as long as [Russian President Vladimir] Putin is in power in Russia - a circumstance shared by millions."

Kasparov retired from competitive chess in 2005 to pursue a career in politics, founding movements that openly opposed Putin before fleeing Russia in 2013.

He has not returned since. Russia classed him as a foreign agent following the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, and subsequently added him to a list of terrorists and extremists in 2024 - both categorisations he rejects.

The other reported target, Ponomarev, was the only Russian MP who voted against the illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and later went into exile in Ukraine.

He declined to confirm or deny to the Moscow Times whether he had been tipped off about the alleged plot but said the allegations marked "a new level of escalation" by Russia.

A network of individuals working for the Russian intelligence services has operated since at least 2024, the US Justice Department said.

It said the so-called RIS Network had been conspiring and conducting attacks and murders on Russian dissidents and defectors around the world.

Five alleged members of the network had been accused of operating "as part of a global assassination network that reached into the United States, attempting to recruit US citizens and foreigners to carry out killings at the behest of the Kremlin", Assistant Attorney General for national security John A Eisenberg said.

The five people alleged to be responsible for organising the plots are Yuri Khrameev, Kirill Khrameev, Oemis Romagoza Durruthy, Yaidel Delgado Suarez and Angel Eduardo Castro.

All five remain at large, the Justice Department said.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when the indictment was unsealed that he would not comment on the charges until he had heard or seen "any credible evidence" or "tangible facts".

The clerk has been deported to India, the Justice Department said.A U Visa is a temporary US immigration status that is reserved for victims of certain crimes who have suffered mental or physical abuse and have been helpful to law enforcement or government officials in the investigation or prosecution of criminal activity. The U Visa provides a path to a Green Card and eventually US citizenship.Staged robbery at a convenience storeOn March 9, 2025, Birenkumar Rameshbhai Patel, also known as “Mike Patel,” and a convenience store clerk staged a robbery at a convenience store in Fairfield County. Patel also arrived at the scene and attempted to explain the robbery.Officers reviewed surveillance video of the event, which appeared to show a robbery, but further review showed that the robbery was staged to make it appear that the store clerk was the victim. Patel acted as the robber and attempted to disguise himself by covering his face and wearing a jacket with long sleeves.On March 25, 2025, Patel and the clerk requested a copy of the incident report as that is a necessary document for the visa application. On April 3, 2025, Patel and/or the clerk mailed a federal certification to the Fairfield County Sheriff’s Department requesting that the head of that department sign a form acknowledging that the clerk was the victim of a “felonious assault.” Officials determined that the store clerk was a citizen of India and that a U Visa would have allowed him to remain in the US legally.Patel faces a maximum penalty of 10 years in federal prison. He also faces a fine of up to $250,000, restitution, three years of supervision to follow the term of imprisonment, the department said. United States District Judge Joseph A. articles.title: Evan Gershkovich details Russian arrest, reveals moment that nearly broke him during wrongful detention
articles.summary: Evan Gershkovich revealed in his new book "This Cursed Beautiful Land" how an FSB setup led to his arrest and the moment that nearly broke him.
articles.body: Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, who was detained by Russia for more than a year before being freed in a massive prisoner swap in 2024, spoke to "Fox & Friends" on Thursday about his arrest in Russia. Gershkovich discussed his new book, "This Cursed Beautiful Land," a firsthand account of the ordeal. "I and a colleague of mine were reporting on basically how Russia was prepping to defend. They were changing their economy to a military footing, and I was meeting with a source of a colleague of mine who we thought was legitimate. We had been speaking to him for four years at that point, and it turned out it was a setup," Gershkovich told "Fox & Friends," describing how he ended up being wrongfully detained. Host Brian Kilmeade pointed to an excerpt in the book that described Gershkovich's realization that the men arresting him were from the FSB, the successor to the Soviet-era KGB, and not just police. "At that moment, when you hear FSB, you understand that, as I write, it's not a misunderstanding," Gershkovich said. "When it's the FSB, you understand it's a high-level planned operation. And I'm taken out in a hood to a van, asked who I work for, I say the Wall Street Journal, the hood comes back on, my midsection is pummeled by the security agents, hood comes back off, they ask who I work for, and that's when it dawns on me, that OK they're accusing me of espionage." He said he was "obviously" scared at that point, and said, "When I get to the station, they just calmly hand me my charges, and they tell me I'm accused of espionage," Gershkovich said. "And there's also this moment that obviously the source, Pavel, stepping away out into the crowd. At that point, I realized, oh, this was a setup and this was a setup for a swap, clearly," he continued. US MARINE VETERAN RELEASED FROM RUSSIAN PRISON AFTER 1,666 DAYS OF DETENTION Gershkovich, 34, was arrested on March 29, 2023, while reporting on a trip to the Ural Mountains city of Yekaterinburg and accused of espionage. The Biden administration declared him "wrongfully detained," and The Wall Street Journal and U.S. government both emphatically denied the charge, which was widely condemned as a thinly disguised effort to take the reporter hostage. After more than a year of delays, he was convicted in 2024 in a closed court of "gathering secret information" and sentenced to 16 years at a penal colony. Wall Street Journal leaders blasted the "sham conviction" and repeatedly called for his immediate release while his friends, family and the journalism community worked to keep his name in the spotlight. FREED MARINE RETURNS HOME 'VERY FRAIL' AFTER RUSSIAN 'NIGHTMARE' AS FAMILY ADVOCATE URGES TRUMP TO FREE OTHERS Kilmeade asked Gershkovich to describe the moment that almost broke him while in a Russian prison. He said he could see what the Biden administration was trying to do to bring him home through a potential prisoner exchange involving the U.S., Russia and Germany. AMERICAN EX-MARINE FEARED NEAR DEATH AFTER WEEKS IN CATATONIC STATE IN RUSSIAN PRISON "It's around the winter where a deal is starting to come together where Paul Whelan, who was also arrested on espionage charges in Russia, and myself are going to be traded for, or a deal would be put to the Russians for myself and Paul Whelan and the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny to be released from Russia, and Vadim Krasikov, the FSB assassin who had been arrested in Germany and was convicted to life in prison there, would be going back to Russia," Gershkovich said. However, he said that while he was out on a walk, he heard on the radio that Navalny had been killed. "I'm out on a walk, it's February. It's really cold. We usually get to listen to a news station called Relax FM. We listen to music. Suddenly the radio station changes. It switches to the news station and it's announced that Alexei Navalny has been killed. At that moment, it's really bleak for me. I think, 'Okay, there's no way I'm getting home now,'" he said. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Gershkovich, along with former U.S. Marine Paul Whelan, was finally freed as part of a massive multinational prisoner swap in August 2024. articles.title: ‘She was pure love’: Renee Good’s partner makes first public comments as family sues U.S. government, ICE officer over her killing
articles.summary: The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January, spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits.
articles.body: The partner of Renee Good, a Minneapolis woman who was fatally shot by an immigration officer in January, spoke publicly about her death for the first time Thursday as the family announced that they have filed two federal civil lawsuits. “She was pure love, and she was funny, and she was smart, and she was gorgeous,” Becca Good said at a press conference, becoming emotional as she discussed attending back-to-school night and preparing to celebrate Halloween with their children alone. “Every single one of these moments for all of her babies and for everyone up here was a monumental moment, and she should be here for all of them. We were all robbed,” she said. Earlier in the press conference, attorneys for Renee Good’s family announced lawsuits alleging wrongful death and excessive force in her Jan. 7 death. One lawsuit seeks to hold the United States liable under the Federal Tort Claims Act for the actions of federal agents. It alleges wrongful death, battery, assault, false imprisonment, emotional distress and negligence. The second suit names Jonathan Ross, the Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer who shot Good, as well as several federal officials, including White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem. “Every morning she’s my first thought. I think about how the kids are growing up without their mama, and how I’ll grow old without the love of my life,” Becca Good said. Renee Good’s brother, Brent Ganger, said her death was “completely senseless.” “We file these two lawsuits today to put officials on notice that we have not forgotten,” he said. The Department of Homeland Security and the White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment. A representative for Ross could not immediately be identified. Good, 37, was fatally shot in the driver’s seat of her SUV during a Jan. 7 encounter with Ross. The killing occurred about a month after the Trump administration deployed 3,000 immigration agents to the Twin Cities in what officials have dubbed Operation Metro Surge. Agents descended on Minnesota after right-wing influencers drew attention to a state fraud scandal involving Somali nationals. The operation triggered massive protests and significant pushback from state leaders. It ended in February. The shooting was captured on cellphone video. It showed Good’s partner, Becca Good, standing outside the SUV calling Ross “big boy” and telling him to remove the covering from his face. Other officers at the scene could be heard telling Good to get out of the car. In the video, Good is seen turning the steering wheel away from Ross and beginning to drive. Multiple gunshots can be heard in the video before Good’s SUV crashes into a parked car. In a separate video recorded by Ross, a male voice could be heard saying “f-----g b----” moments before the crash. Trump administration figures, including President Donald Trump and Noem, defended Ross’ actions and claimed Good was an agitator who tried to run over the officer with her vehicle. Witnesses told NBC News at the time that Ross didn’t appear to be in the direct path of the SUV. Noem said Ross was treated at a hospital for injuries he sustained in the incident and was released soon after. A DHS official previously told NBC News that Ross sustained internal bleeding but did not elaborate on his injuries. Attorney Antonio M. Romanucci, who is representing Good’s family, said he hopes the lawsuits “are the beginning of the ultimate legal weapon in uncovering the truth behind this unlawful use of deadly force and the nefarious conspiracies behind the invasion of American cities by American law enforcement officers.” Weeks after Good’s killing, Customs and Border Protection agents shot and killed Alex Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse, in Minneapolis.

articles.title: “I could not understand what the tourist said”: How Harekala Hajabba turned one painful moment into a mission to build a school for children in his village
articles.summary: For most people, a language barrier is a small inconvenience.
articles.body: For most people, a language barrier is a small inconvenience. For Harekala Hajabba, one such moment became the beginning of a mission that would change the lives of hundreds of children. Hajabba was selling oranges near a bus stand in Mangaluru when a foreign tourist approached him and asked him something in English. He could not understand a single word. He could not answer the question either. That moment made him think about his own life. Hajabba had never gone to school. He knew what it meant to grow up without education, and he did not want children in his village to face the same disadvantage. So, an orange seller with very little money decided to build a school. What followed was a remarkable journey of saving small amounts from his daily earnings, facing doubts and criticism, finding support and eventually turning an impossible-looking dream into reality. His efforts later earned him the Padma Shri.He had no education, but he understood its valueHajabba grew up in Harekala village near Mangaluru, Karnataka, in a financially difficult family. He could not attend school and started working at a young age. For years, selling oranges was his livelihood. His earnings were modest, but he continued saving whatever he could. The encounter with the foreign tourist made him realise how deeply his lack of education had affected him. He could not speak English, but the incident was about more than one language. It reminded him that education could open doors that poverty had kept closed. Instead of simply feeling helpless, Hajabba decided to do something for children in his village. His idea was ambitious: build a school so that children would not have to grow up without access to education as he had.It was not an easy dream for an orange seller. There were people who laughed at his plans and did not believe that someone with so little money could build a school. But Hajabba continued with his efforts. He saved money from his business and approached people for help. Slowly, the idea that had once seemed impossible began taking shape.An orange seller kept saving until his dream became a schoolHajabba’s journey was not about suddenly receiving a large donation and building a school overnight. It was built through years of persistence. His efforts to establish a school began in the 1990s. Initially, classes were held in a madrasa building. Eventually, the school moved into its own premises, giving children from Harekala and nearby areas an opportunity to study closer to home. The school’s development was a major achievement for someone who had never experienced formal education himself. But perhaps the most powerful part of his story is that Hajabba did not stop at simply creating a building. His focus remained on ensuring that children from his village had access to education.He continued selling oranges even after his work became known beyond Karnataka. His story also challenged a common idea about who can create social change. Hajabba was not a wealthy businessman or an influential politician. He was an ordinary man who earned a modest living and decided to put his savings towards something he believed his community desperately needed. One small decision followed another. One saved rupee became part of a larger contribution. One conversation became a campaign. And one personal disappointment eventually became an opportunity for an entire village.From a bus stand vendor to Padma Shri awardeeHajabba’s work eventually attracted national attention. In 2020, he was selected for the Padma Shri for his contribution to social work. The recognition brought his extraordinary journey into the national spotlight. For someone who had once been unable to understand a tourist’s question, receiving one of India’s highest civilian honours was a remarkable turn in his life. But the award was never the real purpose of his work. The school was. Hajabba’s story continues to resonate because it is not simply about overcoming poverty or receiving recognition. It is about what happens when someone turns a personal struggle into a reason to help others.He could have remembered that encounter with the tourist as an embarrassing moment and moved on. Instead, he asked himself what could be done so that children in his village would have opportunities that he never received. That question became bigger than him. Today, Harekala Hajabba is remembered not only as the man who sold oranges at a Mangaluru bus stand but also as the man who used those earnings to invest in education. His journey carries a simple message: you do not always need wealth, power or a privileged background to create change. Sometimes, all it takes is the decision to turn one difficult experience into a purpose. For Hajabba, one unanswered question became the beginning of a school. articles.title: 'Don't want BJP to come': AIMIM's Owaisi leaves door open for alliance ahead of 2027 UP elections
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Thursday said his party was open to forming an electoral alliance with other political parties in Uttar Pradesh
articles.body: NEW DELHI: AIMIM chief Asaduddin Owaisi on Thursday said his party was open to forming an electoral alliance with other political parties in Uttar Pradesh ahead of next year’s Assembly elections, saying it did not want the BJP to return to power in the state for a third consecutive term.Addressing a press conference, Owaisi said AIMIM would contest the elections “with all our force” and would announce any alliance once it was finalised.“We don't want the BJP to come to power in Uttar Pradesh for the third time. In order to stop this from happening, we are open for alliance. What else can we say?” Owaisi said, according to new agency PTI.He referred to AIMIM’s experience in Bihar, where four of the party’s five MLAs joined the RJD in June 2022. The move enabled the RJD to reclaim its position as the single largest party in the Bihar Assembly.Owaisi said AIMIM had sought only six seats in Bihar previously and alleged that its concerns had not received the same political attention as similar developments involving other parties.“We fought again and people voted for us. We bagged five seats there,” he said.“It is up to them (political parties in UP) now. We will contest the elections there with all our force, and whenever an alliance happens, we will let you know. We will decide our fate and make our leadership,” Owaisi added.The Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections are scheduled to be held early next year to elect all 403 members of the House.Owaisi questions opposition’s claims over electionsOwaisi also criticised political parties that have attributed electoral defeats both to AIMIM’s presence in contests and to alleged vote theft.“The opposition once said that they lost the elections because we (AIMIM) were in the fray. Sometimes, they say that they lost the elections because of vote theft. How is this possible? They should be clear,” he said.Owaisi alleges UCC aims to impose Hindu lawsOwaisi also criticised the implementation of the Uniform Civil Code (UCC) in some states and alleged that the move was aimed at turning India into a “Hindu Rashtra”.He claimed that the UCC laws in Uttarakhand, Assam and Gujarat were a “cut and paste” of the Hindu Marriage Act and Hindu Succession Act, and questioned their applicability to Muslims.“The Maharashtra government is working on UCC now. But the laws in Uttarakhand, Assam and Gujarat are the same. It is just a 'cut and paste' of Hindu Marriage Act and Hindu Succession Act,” Owaisi said.He said tribals had been excluded from the UCC in Uttarakhand and Gujarat because of differences in their religious and social practices, and argued that Muslims faced a similar issue.“When marriage in Islam is a contract and it is a bond for life time, how can Hindu Marriage Act be imposed on me? Why should I marry according to it?” he asked.Owaisi further alleged that UCC provisions could affect inheritance arrangements and said the move violated Articles 25, 26 and 29 of the Constitution.“BJP leaders say that women should get equal share (in property). In Assam, Uttarakhand and Gujarat where UCC was implemented, the power of will helps a person give away (the property) to just one son when he has three. UCC is an effort to implement the laws of Hindus over Muslims. This is a violation of Article 25, 26 and 29 (of the Indian Constitution). It is a way to make India a Hindu Rashtra,” he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Flydubai stabbing: What happens when a pilot turns violent mid-flight?
articles.summary: Flydubai FZ1073 raises questions about cockpit security, pilot vetting and threats from inside the flight deck.
articles.body:
On Wednesday morning, a co-pilot aboard a Flydubai plane stabbed the captain in what is believed to have been a foiled attempt to crash the flight with more than 170 people on board, en route from Dubai to Israel’s Tel Aviv .

As the plane plunged , within a minute, to half its altitude amid the commotion as it approached Jordanian airspace, the captain managed to unlock the door to the cockpit, and a group of passengers and crew members stormed inside and overpowered the attacker, who was reportedly attempting to damage the controls.

The aircraft also emitted an emergency distress signal during the incident.

Another pilot on board managed to take control of the aircraft and land it safely in Saudi Arabia’s Tabuk.

While the United Arab Emirates, the airline’s host country, has begun an investigation into what happened, Saudi authorities are questioning the co-pilot who allegedly attacked the captain. The attacker was also injured and is now in Saudi custody. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the country would follow the investigation and “possibly participate”.

Israel has claimed the incident on board the plane, the majority of whose passengers were Israeli, was a “terrorist” attack and an attempt to crash the aircraft.

Meanwhile, the incident on board Flydubai flight FZ1073 has raised a host of uncomfortable questions in the civil aviation industry, chief among them: how safe is a commercial aircraft when one of its own pilots turns violent?

How has aviation changed since the attacks of 9/11?

Twenty-five years ago, the September 11 attacks on the United States, which killed nearly 3,000 people, changed the civil aviation industry.

That day, al-Qaeda-affiliated hijackers took control of four commercial planes as they were in the air, crashing two into the twin towers of New York’s World Trade Center on Manhattan island, and another into the Pentagon. A fourth crashed in Pennsylvania after passengers overwhelmed the hijackers.

The attacks transformed aviation security, which stepped up its focus on preventing unauthorised access to aircraft flight decks, as well as strengthening security and boarding procedures within airports.

Within months, the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) had overhauled the global aviation rules, extending security measures for domestic flights and introducing bulletproof, reinforced cockpit doors, personnel vetting and airport identity checks.

The most consequential physical change was the reinforced, lockable cockpit door, designed to resist forcible intrusion, followed by a mandatory 100 percent screening of checked baggage.

Airports increased employee screening, baggage and cargo security, and aircraft protection, while ICAO introduced mandatory security audits to assess how countries were implementing the new global standards.

In 2015, Germanwings Flight 9525’s first officer Andreas Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit and deliberately flew the Airbus A320 they were piloting into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board.

France’s BEA determined that the aviation industry’s medical-certification system had failed to prevent a pilot experiencing a serious mental disorder from operating with a licence.

Following that incident, the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) temporarily recommended that at least two authorised people remain in the cockpit at all times. But the following year, the EASA moved the rule to a risk-based approach only, allowing airlines to adopt equivalent safeguards based on operational risks.

The Germanwings incident also triggered broader measures in Europe: from 2018, airlines were required to conduct psychological assessments before pilots began flying and introduce psychoactive substance and alcohol testing.

Some flights also carry air marshals – or “in-flight security officers” – who are generally covert, armed law-enforcement officers placed on selected flights depending on a country’s threat assessment.

Cockpit doors are made to be particularly difficult to penetrate, as standard. On modern commercial aircraft, the cockpit door is built to be a heavy-duty composite structure mounted inside a reinforced frame, and electronically controlled, designed to resist forcible intrusion and penetration by small firearms. The cockpit door can usually only be opened from the inside.

On Boeing 737 aircraft, the flight-deck access system normally remains in AUTO mode during the flight, keeping the reinforced cockpit door locked. Cabin crew can ask pilots to grant them entry through the access system.

ICAO standards require that such doors can be locked or unlocked from either pilot station.

An emergency keypad also allows crew to initiate an emergency entry sequence to enter the cockpit. If a functioning pilot does not cancel the emergency request, the system would permit emergency access, but only after a built-in delay.

These systems are designed to keep an attacker out of the cockpit – not to stop a threat already inside it.

On the Flydubai flight on Wednesday, the Indian pilot who had been stabbed reportedly managed to open the cockpit door during the attack, which “enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker – preventing a catastrophic midair disaster”, Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who hailed the captain as a “hero”, told the media.

What happens once a pilot raises the alarm?

It depends on the type of emergency in the aircraft. Under ICAO procedures, a crew can declare an emergency by radio using the signal “MAYDAY”.

In cases of medical or technical issues, pilots use the transponder code 7700 to alert air traffic control that they need to land as soon as possible, said Saj Ahmad, chief analyst at StrategicAero Research, a London-based aviation consultancy. “Often, passengers are oblivious to this as there’s no need for alarm,” he added. This is the code that the Flydubai craft emitted as it was descending sharply, according to the flight monitoring service Flightradar24.

If the emergency is an attack or hijacking, the aircraft can transmit transponder code 7500, which flags the flight to air traffic controllers as being subject to unlawful interference, added Ahmad. “The crew can also communicate the nature of the threat and their intentions in plain language,” he said. The Flydubai craft switched to this code a few minutes after issuing the first code, according to flight data.

If code 7500 is the input, air traffic control is alerted to an “interference with the flight or a possible hijack in progress, and often ATC will divert other jets away so that the squawking jet can land”.

Flydubai’s 7700 emergency warning was sent at 5:28 GMT, followed by 7500 at 5:35 GMT, according to FlightRadar24, leading to the initial reports of a possible hijacking of the flight en route to Israel.

The cabin crew’s duties in such emergencies cover pilot incapacitation and security threats, including protecting the flight deck and communicating with the operating pilot.

But the nature of violence in or near the flight deck can vary, Ahmad said, as “often the strategy is to open the door so that other crew members can assist”.

Violence between the pilots inside the cockpit leads to a worst-case scenario, he said: “Where both pilots are unable to fly, the consequences are pretty self-evident if no one is flying the airplane.”

The Flydubai aeroplane was ultimately safely landed by two other pilots who were on board. That is the equivalent of lightning striking once, Ahmad suggested. “It is frightening to think of what the outcome would have been if those additional pilots were not there to take control.”

Before being granted a Class 1 medical certificate necessary for their licence, pilots undergo an aeromedical assessment covering vision, hearing, cardiovascular and neurological health, and other conditions that could cause sudden incapacitation.

Aviation security rules also require background checks for all personnel who have unescorted access to security-restricted areas.

“Frequency of health checks varies, but standard health checks like height, weight, blood pressure, psychological testing, psychometric testing, as well as fitness, are minimum evaluations that all pilots undergo, as well as drug and drink testing,” said Ahmad of StrategicAero Research.

After the Flydubai incident, Ahmad said that “Israel will probably insist on specific nationalities for flight crew going forward” as well.

Israel has already said it will ramp up security checks on pilots flying into the country. “Every pilot that is going to be flying into Israel, we are going to know the pilots’ identities, know who they are, and do some type of security check,” Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office, said.

“I can see Israel demanding details of flight crews before a flight even departs, with full and even more invasive security checks and ensuring pilots who fly there are from nations where diplomatic relations with Israel exist,” Ahmad told Al Jazeera.

“This sort of cross-vetting isn’t usually a thing, but after this Flydubai incident, it makes sense now to explore whether wider sharing of pilot details and backgrounds to other aviation regulators in other countries could be standardised to further advance safety measures,” he added.

Pilot-on-pilot violence is not completely unheard of. There have been punches thrown, collars grabbed and arguments. But a co-pilot stabbing his captain in mid-flight in an attempt to seize the aircraft is an extraordinarily rare form of aviation security incident, analysts said.

articles.title: Moroccan intelligence uses surveillance to ‘silence’ journalists: Amnesty
articles.summary: Probe finds spyware, hidden microphones and infected phones used to surveil journalists, activists, rights defenders.
articles.body:
Amnesty International has denounced Morocco’s intelligence agency for using spyware, hidden microphones and pre-infected phones in the “unlawful surveillance” of journalists and human rights defenders.

Moroccan authorities host an “expansive and vast” surveillance apparatus that they use to “ultimately silence journalists, activists and other critical voices”, the rights NGO said in a report published on Thursday.

The report, Inside Morocco’s surveillance machine, is based on the testimony of a former employee of the Moroccan domestic intelligence service (DGST), as well as leaked documents and journalistic investigations.

NGOs, including Amnesty, have for years accused Morocco of using Pegasus spyware, developed by the Israeli NSO Group, to monitor journalists, activists and political figures.

Rabat has repeatedly denied using spyware against its citizens. Amnesty said it wrote to Moroccan authorities four weeks before publication and received no response. Al Jazeera could not immediately reach Moroccan officials for comment.

In its report, Amnesty identified the DGST as the body responsible for deploying Pegasus in Morocco, saying the agency used the spyware against activists and journalists between 2017 and 2021.

Amnesty said Moroccan authorities combined “high-tech tools” like Pegasus with more traditional techniques like tailing and wiretapping.

“People are secretly videoed and audio recorded in detention, in their own offices and cars, and even in their own bedrooms,” the report says, citing the whistleblower.

“Phone calls are systematically recorded and spied upon,” and “shops sell mobile phones pre-infected with malware by DGST agents”.

The personal data collected on activists and human rights defenders is used to fuel public smear campaigns against them, according to the NGO.

The whistleblower said the agency infected internet cafes with remote-controlled spyware, and that devices were physically compromised at airports. He added that microphones were hidden in the light fixtures of the apartment of journalist Omar Radi, who was later imprisoned.

Amnesty said it matched 103 Moroccan phone numbers entered into the Pegasus system between September and December 2017 to specific individuals. Of these, 65 were civil society members, including 34 human rights defenders and 22 journalists and media workers. Another 25 were political figures or officials, and five were diplomats or representatives of international organisations.

“These records show the phone numbers of prominent human rights defenders and journalists were among the first to be entered into the Pegasus system,” said Donncha O Cearbhaill, head of Amnesty’s Security Lab.

Amnesty said it also found evidence of spyware delivered over the state-owned Maroc Telecom network, and that Morocco bought tools from companies based in Israel, the European Union and the United States.

“Morocco has wholly embraced techno-authoritarian practices,” Amnesty Secretary-General Agnes Callamard said.

Amnesty called on Morocco to end the surveillance and on states to halt spyware exports to the country until human rights safeguards are in place.

The investigation was part of a collaboration with 14 media organisations coordinated by Forbidden Stories.

articles.title: In 1999, an Anaheim architect began building a backyard Disneyland; 27 years later, his miniature world includes a garden railroad and a 350-LED light show
articles.summary: Discover how David Sheegog's 27-year project turned his Anaheim backyard into a stunning miniature Disneyland, featuring castles, themed buildings, and a captivating water and light show with 350 individual LED lights.
articles.body: For David Sheegog, Disneyland did not end at the park gates. The architect took the idea home, first to his dining room table and eventually across almost every corner of his Anaheim Hills backyard.What began as a garden railway project in the late 1990s has grown over 27 years into a miniature Disney world, complete with castles, trains, themed buildings and an aerial skyway. Its latest addition is Pixie Hollow, a water and light show featuring 350 LED pixel lights that can be programmed individually.Sheegog, now 70, began the project while he and his wife Frances were homeschooling their children at their Anaheim, California, home. He wanted the backyard to become a “living laboratory” where the children could explore science and nature.Garden railroading soon became part of that planBefore construction began, Sheegog spent about two years developing a miniature version of the backyard on the family’s dining room table. He built the model from clay and used the architectural computer programme he worked with to design the railway track layout.“For about two years, between ‘97 and ‘99, we had a model of our backyard on our dining room table,” Sheegog told PEOPLE.The model helped persuade Frances to go along with the idea. But Sheegog still needed a theme for the railway and landscape.A family trip to Disney World eventually supplied it.While watching home video from the trip, Sheegog noticed Snow White’s cottage being built in the background as his children prepared to leave. The sight helped him decide where the project would go.“Somewhere in that period, I decided that the theme would be Disney and so I started making the landmarks,” Sheegog told the outlet .A railway becomes a miniature Disney worldConstruction began in 1999, and Sheegog showed the first version of the project to friends and family in 2000.Rather than relying entirely on small prefabricated buildings, he wanted to create larger structures himself.“Most of the garden railroads I had seen people had bought pre-made kits of little plastic buildings that are all about 12 inches by 8 inches,” Sheegog told the Los Angeles Times. “They look like premade little buildings, like a barber shop. No.”His own designs were considerably larger. “I wanted to build this from scratch, and wanted them to be impressive, like 5 feet across and 4 feet tall. Or in the case of one of our castles, 7 feet tall,” he told the newspaper.The garden now includes miniature versions of Sleeping Beauty’s Castle, the Haunted Mansion and the Disneyland Railroad, along with Casey Jr. Circus Train.Sheegog has also built structures based on characters and settings from Disney and Pixar films, including Beast’s Castle, Prince Eric’s Seaside Villa from The Little Mermaid and Carl Fredricksen’s house from Up.Some components were made from sets, others were built from scratch, while more recent additions have used 3D printing.350 LEDs power the newest attractionThe latest addition has pushed the project into more elaborate territory.Pixie Hollow, which debuted on May 9, features a water and light show using 350 LED pixel lights. Each light is independently programmed, according to Sheegog.“It’s the most complicated thing I’ve ever done,” Sheegog told PEOPLE.The project involved around 13 consultants, including animators, music arrangers and contractors, he told the magazine.The technical work is a significant departure from the clay model that started the project more than two decades ago. Yet Sheegog continues to treat the backyard as an evolving project rather than a finished attraction.He is also considering additional interactive experiences involving laser shows, holograms, animations and live actors, according to the Daily Mail.Open houses sell out in secondsThe backyard is normally private, but the Sheegogs open it to visitors several weekends each spring and autumn.There is no admission charge, but places can be difficult to secure, with all 2,000 spots for one autumn open house disappearing in 56 seconds.The events have also brought visitors with their own connections to Disneyland.Speaking to the Los Angeles Times, Sheegog recalled one woman who was nearly 100 and had worked at the park on its opening day. She had spent her career there and began crying while recounting memories from her youth.For Sheegog, those reactions have become as important as the structures he builds.“My favorite thing isn't something we've built, it's seeing how people enjoy it,” Sheegog told the Daily Mail. “When we have open houses and I see families interacting with each other, sometimes I just sit on the bench and watch the people.”Why the project keeps growingSheegog has considered retirement, but that has not stopped him from planning new additions.He told the Los Angeles Times that he hoped to continue the project for at least another decade, with plans to build during his 60s and operate it through his 70s and potentially into his 80s.The attraction has also become a way for people who grew up around Disneyland to reconnect with memories of the park.“We grew up with the park, and it has a certain sentimental niche in your psyche,” Sheegog told the Los Angeles Times. “People just want to be around it, and our place provides an outlet for that.”After 27 years, the backyard is still changing. The railway that began as a family project has become a detailed miniature landscape, and the latest 350-LED show suggests Sheegog is still finding new ways to expand it.Sheegog says watching families “interacting and having fun” remains the reason he keeps doing it.You use AI every day.
