articles.title: Rowan Rieve, 12, of Sugar Hill, Georgia, raised $22.25 at a lemonade stand while battling brain cancer; his gift inspired a $100,000 donation, and his city later honoured him after his death
articles.summary: A neighbourhood lemonade stand can seem like a small summer ritual: a folding table, a pitcher and a few coins dropped into a jar.
articles.body: A neighbourhood lemonade stand can seem like a small summer ritual: a folding table, a pitcher and a few coins dropped into a jar. For Rowan Daniel Rieve, however, it became the beginning of a much larger legacy. While undergoing years of treatment for brain cancer, the 12-year-old from Sugar Hill, Georgia, decided to raise money for childhood cancer research. The stand brought in just $22.25, but the gesture eventually inspired an anonymous donation of more than $100,000 in his honour, states an online report by North Gwinnett Voice.The report adds that Rowan died in July, following a four-year battle with cancer. A month later, his hometown marked what would have been his 13th birthday by proclaiming August 4 Rowan Daniel Rieve Day and recognising him as a Sugar Hill Heron.A childhood interrupted by cancerAs per the report, Rowan's cancer journey began in August 2021, when he was eight years old. After experiencing repeated vomiting and growing increasingly weak, he was taken to an emergency department, where a CT scan revealed a golf-ball-sized blockage in his brain.He underwent emergency neurosurgery and was diagnosed with medulloblastoma, a form of paediatric brain cancer. Weeks in hospital were followed by daily proton radiation and more than a year of chemotherapy. With support from Alex's Lemonade Stand Foundation's Travel For Care programme, his family was also able to manage the demands of travelling for treatment.For a time, there was hope that treatment had ended. But an MRI in 2023 revealed another abnormality. Doctors later diagnosed a high-grade glioma, leading to another surgery, radiation and chemotherapy. Rowan was also found to have Li-Fraumeni syndrome, an inherited condition associated with an increased risk of cancer and the disease returned again in 2025.Turning a small fundraiser into a lasting impactDespite repeated treatment, Rowan continued attending school and taking part in the activities he loved. He played trombone, enjoyed board and card games and spent time with friends and his younger brother.Then came the lemonade stand. After learning that funding for paediatric brain tumour research had been lost, Rowan and several neighbourhood friends decided to do something about it. Their first effort raised only $22.25. Its impact, however, far exceeded the amount collected. The fundraiser attracted attention and ultimately led an anonymous donor to contribute more than $100,000 towards childhood cancer research in Rowan's honour.A legacy built on kindnessRowan's generosity was evident in everyday moments as well. During a family trip to Walt Disney World through Bert's Big Adventure, he noticed a younger child who was nervous about meeting Disney characters. Rowan stayed beside him and helped him feel comfortable. His family also made space for experiences beyond hospitals and treatment, including ziplining, hiking in the Blue Ridge Mountains and walking along beaches.For Sugar Hill, Rowan's legacy now extends beyond his battle with cancer. The city's proclamation highlighted his kindness, perseverance and commitment to helping other children facing similar illnesses.His story began with a $22.25 lemonade stand. It ended with a community remembering a child who, even while facing an extraordinary personal challenge, found a way to make his concern for others part of his own story.Images Courtesy: istock and North Gwinnett VoiceYou use AI every day. articles.title: Shropshire Oktoberfest set to welcome thousands to Shrewsbury Quarry
articles.summary: Thousands of people are expected in Shrewsbury's Quarry park over the weekend.
articles.body:
Thousands of people are expected in Shrewsbury this weekend for the annual Oktoberfest.

The event, which started in 2017, is a spin on the traditional German beer festivals.

It will take place in The Quarry on Friday and Saturday with more than 150 drinks available from both local and German producers, as well as live music, street food, stand-up comedy and a silent disco.

Among the performers are the Oompah band Vorsprung Durch, who will perform on Saturday afternoon.

The group plays traditional German polkas and waltzes, as well as arrangements of popular songs like The White Stripes' Seven Nation Army and Madness' Baggy Trousers, which frontman Neil Fury introduces as "Baggy Lederhosen".

Band member Lisa Kendall said Vorsprung Durch was formed in 2013 after the musicians got together and "thought what would be really cool would be a bit of beer drinking" and getting into the Oktoberfest spirit.

"You've got to be ready for the Prost and the cheers and encourage everyone," Kendall said, adding that people did not have to drink alcohol to join in.

Visitors to the festival can choose from tipples including beer, cider, gin and wine, or opt for a non-alcoholic option.

Street food sold at the event is set to include bratwurst, burgers, chips and churros.

The rest of the live music line-up includes covers bands such as Skaburst and Hot Rox, the alt-folk trio Two Blank Pages and comedy band Asparagus & The Kilburn Habit.

Performing in the festival's comedy live lounge on Saturday are acts such as Britain's Got Talent stars Daliso Chaponda and Maddy Muden, as well as stand-up names like James Dowdeswell and Jo Enright.

Other activities to enjoy include face painting and "carpool karaoke".

articles.title: Lib Dems criticise Ed Davey over pension triple lock response
articles.summary: Sir Ed questioned the PM's plans to change the triple lock, telling the BBC removing it "would put more pensioners into poverty".
articles.body:
Liberal Democrat MPs have criticised their party leader over his defence of the pension triple lock.

Senior Lib Dems, who are on the party's frontbench, have privately attacked Sir Ed Davey for his response to the prime minister's plans to adjust the policy , which guarantees the state pension goes up each year in line with either inflation, wage increases, or 2.5% – whichever is highest.

They joined unsolicited criticism in public and private from others in the party, with one saying the majority of Lib Dem MPs disagree with their leader.

It comes after Sir Ed told the BBC removing the triple lock "would put more pensioners into poverty".

"This would mean people who are working hard now - the millennials - when they retire would have a very poor pension," he told the Today programme.

Under Andy Burnham's plan - which he hopes will raise £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s - the automatic annual link with average earnings would be removed from 2030 so the state pension rises with at least 2.5% or inflation, whichever is higher.

"His proposals are to deal with social care in the next decade when it needs to be done now," Sir Ed said.

"It's a little bit of a vibe. It's not a solution," he said.

But multiple Lib Dems at different levels have now criticised Sir Ed's response.

Could changing the pension triple lock pay for Burnham's big social care plan?

What is the triple lock and why are people talking about it?

A Lib Dem MP contacted the BBC after Sir Ed's interview to say the majority of the parliamentary party would not support opposing Burnham's changes to the triple lock.

Another, Tom Gordon, who represents Harrogate & Knaresborough, said Sir Ed's criticism of Burnham's plan to adjust the triple lock was "nonsense" and "gaslights an entire generation into believing it's for our benefit".

He wrote on X: "The idea that we're keeping the triple lock to help millennials is at best for the birds, and at worst downright insulting. I say that as a millennial."

He added: "Telling millennials we're keeping the triple lock to help us in 30 years' time is nonsense.

"We're on course to be the first generation worse off than our parents. We're locked out of the housing market, paying higher taxes, repaying student loans that never seem to shrink, and putting off having children because of the cost of living."

Vikki Slade, the party's MP for Mid-Dorset and North Poole, said on Bluesky: "Most millennials don't think there will be a state pension when they retire so this isn't being done with them in mind."

She added that she was "proud" of the triple lock when it was introduced by the Conservative-Liberal Democrat coalition government in 2010, "but we must plan for future not venerate the past".

A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "The triple lock has always been controversial.

"It's done a lot of good but its job isn't done yet, so Labour's plan would push too many of today's workers into poverty when they retire.

"We want Andy Burnham to get back around the table so that we can find a lasting consensus on social care with a sustainable funding model - not one pulled out of the pockets of a group of people who can least afford it."

The Lib Dems, and other opposition parties, are battling to respond to a new set of priorities from the Labour government under Burnham.

One frontbench Lib Dem MP told the BBC after Burnham's Labour conference speech: "Lots of us [are] struggling tonight with [a] Labour leader articulating Lib Dem values better than we do."

They pointed to Burnham's promises on electoral reform, social care, the water industry, and relations with Europe - all Lib Dem campaign points in recent years.

"I'm honestly utterly despondent with the state of things," another Lib Dem MP said.

Some senior Lib Dems believe Sir Ed's position as leader has been vulnerable for some time, even if they stressed no challenge is imminent.

"A plausible candidate could take him tomorrow in a bloodless coup," one prominent party figure said.

"But that person hasn't yet revealed themselves as far as I'm aware. Nobody is going to blow anything up without a clear plan to put something in its place."

articles.title: Prince of Wales tells villagers 'holistic' approach is needed on flooding
articles.summary: Prince William visits residents of Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, who have faced four floods in six years.
articles.body:
The Prince of Wales has said a "holistic" approach is needed to tackle severe flooding, as a small Welsh village prepares for the upcoming storm season.

Residents in Skenfrith, Monmouthshire, have faced four major floods in the past six years.

An extreme flood last winter had a devastating impact on the village , when the River Monnow burst its banks after Storm Claudia brought a month's worth of rain in just 24 hours to parts of England and Wales.

Prince William was visiting the area to learn about how communities have been affected by recent flooding and what measures were being taken by local authorities and other agencies to mitigate future incidents.

Over the years, families have reported that their homes and possessions had been destroyed by the floods. In 2019, about 25 homes were evacuated in the village following flooding and a power cut after heavy rain.

The prince sympathised with residents who might be "anxious" about extreme weather events he said were no longer "one in 50-year" occurrences but instead seemed to be happening every year.

On Thursday, the prince spoke to villagers Rod and Helen Wyatt at their garden gate and was told how the water almost topped gravestones in a cemetery opposite during a flood.

The couple have now tiled the ground floor of their house and live with the threat of further flooding.

Rod, who has lived in his home for 10 years, made light of the experience when he told Prince William that, at one point, "we had to give up really, we got two bottles of Prosecco and went to watch Strictly upstairs".

The prince replied: "It must be so demoralising for you now, the worry each year you've got to go through that again, potentially, is becoming more frequent.

"They keep talking about a one in 50-year event, it doesn't make sense anymore.

"It might be in the researching and scientific point of view - it's happening every year now, it's mad.

"So, it's trying to understand how we can do a better holistic view of the whole catchment area, so we're dealing with the whole problem."

He listed a number of ideas, from "slowing the water down" using farming landscaping remedies, to tree planting and better monitoring "so we know when things might be getting worse".

Prince William discussed the ideas in detail while later meeting representatives from environmental charity Stump Up for Trees at Great Tre-Rhew Farm in Monmouthshire.

The charity, founded in 2020, aims to plant one million native trees across south Wales and Bannau Brycheiniog, also known as the Brecon Beacons .

The prince joined volunteers harvesting seeds from a field maple tree and planted a sessile oak tree - designated as the national tree of Wales.

To access the trees, he had to climb over a barbed wire fence and use a small step, joking that he did not want to rip his trousers.

As he harvested seeds from the tree, he noted he was taller than others present, adding: "I'm going to reach up here and get these higher ones."

The charity collected 35,000 seeds last year that were used to grow new trees for planting, and hopes to increase this to 60,000 this year.

The prince spoke to Kate and Jim Beavan, of Great Tre-Rhew Farm, and Jenny Knight, the director of Stump Up for Trees.

After the visit, Knight paid tribute to Prince William for "looking at not just the problems but the solutions as well".

Representatives from the Duchy of Cornwall also joined the visit to share learning about nature recovery, climate-resilient forestry and to start a long-term partnership.

Knight added "knowledge exchange is so valuable" and said working together across different areas would have a greater impact.

At the end of the conversation, William discussed his enjoyment of cider, which is made on the farm.

"He said 'one pint a day keeps the doctor away'," Knight said.

Prince William also visited Herefordshire and met farmer Harry Davies, 25, who is set to lead the Duchy of Cornwall's first regenerative farming project on a 25-year lease at the 900-acre farm.

The project aims to improve soil health and make farms more resilient to flooding and drought.

Davies said: "By us being able to hold that water in that soil profile so it doesn't go into our rivers and streams quite so quickly, we should be able to hold the water on our land. Which in the long term will then benefit us when it's hot and dry.

"There seems to be an opportunity to draw on experience from my Grandad's generation, but also a bit of youth and enthusiasm is also needed. I think it's about generations working together, that's just farming."

articles.title: Christa Pike in critical condition after surviving two lethal injections, lawyer says
articles.summary: Pike had been on death row since she was convicted in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.
articles.body:
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike is in "critical condition, receiving life-saving care" at hospital, after surviving two lethal injection attempts, leading the state's governor to halt all executions for the year.

"We don't have a sense of her prognosis or much update on her health at the moment," her lawyer Randy Spivey told reporters on Thursday. "But we do know that that she is alive right now."

Her lawyers are now asking for her sentence to be commuted which was previously denied.

Prison officials injected two lethal doses of pentobarbital to Pike on Wednesday, but she survived and was taken to hospital.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

Her execution was the subject of a last-minute legal battle. This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead on Wednesday evening.

Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer.

She would have been the first woman to be executed in Tennessee for over 200 years.

Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said on Thursday the investigation into Pike's botched execution "will be thorough", adding that "it's going to take time".

"There are a lot of questions," Lee said. "The people of our state deserve to have those questions answered, and that's what this investigation is for."

Lee has not made clear who will conduct the independent review of the state's execution procedures.

His order to pause all executions will overlap with the planned 3 December execution of convicted murderer Gary Sutton.

In court filings, Pike's lawyers said she needed "life-saving measures" after her botched execution.

The Tennessee Department of Correction, which handled the execution, issued a statement defending its handling of the case.

It said in a statement that it "followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office".

"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening."

Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, as per state protocol when the first attempt fails, but was still alive afterwards, according to court filings.

"This execution is causing Ms Pike unnecessary agony and occurring in violation of his right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment," her lawyers said.

The Tennessee attorney general's office said in a statement that it agreed with the decision to call for an investigation, adding: "We need to know what happened."

Pike's attempted execution proceeded after multiple last-minute legal challenges by her lawyers had failed, overturned in the final hour by the US Supreme Court.

Slemmer's mother May Martinez, who was among those who wanted the execution to take place and who travelled to Tennessee to witness it, told NBC News after the botched attempt that "it was a mess".

US Republican Senator Marsha Blackburn, who is running for Tennessee governor, described the situation as "tragic".

"While there should be a thorough review of what happened and why the process failed, the answer is simple: bring back the electric chair," Blackburn said.

Democrat Jerri Green, Blackburn's opponent, criticised her for wanting to "bring back one of the most cruel forms of capital punishment".

"As governor, I would put a moratorium on all future executions," Green said on X.

This is the second time in 2026 Tennessee officials attempted and failed to execute a prisoner.

In May, the execution of Tony Carruthers was called off after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug. Carruthers was given a one-year reprieve.

articles.title: Hundreds of jobs under threat at Grangemouth chemical plant
articles.summary: Syngenta said its Grangemouth operation was no longer 'competitive' due to increasing competition from overseas.
articles.body:
Hundreds of jobs are under threat in Grangemouth after an agricultural chemical firm announced plans to cease operations at the site.

Syngenta said it had been unable to make its business at the plant "competitive" in the face of "increasing international competition".

A spokesperson for the company - which manufactures chemicals used for the protection of crops - said it would enter a consultation period over the move, but added a final decision has yet to be taken.

The Economy Secretary, Stephen Flynn, described the plans as "extremely disappointing".

The UK government's Reindustrialisation Minister, Blair McDougall, said they had worked with Scottish counterparts to "explore every possible avenue" for support, but Syngenta had taken the decision on a commercial basis.

A total of 377 workers are set to be affected by the move.

It comes over a year after Syngenta was awarded £2.2m from Scottish Enterprise to expand production at the site.

New £150m funding package to protect jobs at Grangemouth

Bus firm Alexander Dennis to close Falkirk site with loss of 115 jobs

Syngenta added that it was "committed to genuine consultation" with trade unions over "alternative paths" for the site.

The firm said it had undertaken a "detailed review" of its Grangemouth operation prior to the plans being announced.

It said the Grangemouth site was "significantly more expensive" to operate than other production facilities.

The company added that savings had been identified in some areas of the business, but these fell short in "bridging the site's competitiveness gap".

Mike Hollands, president of Syngenta UK, said: "The workforce at Grangemouth is highly skilled and passionate, but despite all efforts, we have not been able to make the Grangemouth site competitive compared to alternative supply options.

"It is with a very heavy heart that we make this proposal, but we are committed to a constructive consultation and will continue to consider options as part of that process."

It is the latest job loss blow to the area following the closure of the nearby oil refinery in April last year, which also resulted in the loss of about 400 jobs.

In March, bus manufacturer Alexander Dennis announced plans to close its Falkirk plant with 115 roles lost.

The UK government, under then-Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, previously pledged an additional £200m in funding for Grangemouth from the National Wealth Fund.

Flynn said the Scottish government had "strongly opposed" Syngenta's plans.

He said he would continue to press the UK government on the £200m funding pot.

"My thoughts are with the workers, their families and the local community who will be affected by this decision," he said.

"We made clear to Syngenta's board our strong opposition to any potential scale down or closure of their Grangemouth site."

Flynn added: "During this period of consultation, I sincerely hope that the UK government will now provide some of the £200m committed to Grangemouth, since not a single penny has yet been allocated from that fund promised in 2024."

McDougall said the UK government would work with the National Wealth Fund in the coming days to "explore all options for the area".

"I know this will be a deeply concerning time for workers at Syngenta and their families, and I met with the company earlier today to discuss all options for the site and the workforce," he said.

"We will continue to work closely with both of them and look at all options for the site and the workforce."

Scottish Conservative Central Scotland MSP Meghan Gallacher said: "This is another hammer blow for Grangemouth and my thoughts are with the workers who are set to lose their jobs.

"Grangemouth and the surrounding communities have been devastated by the closure of major sites in recent years and this will have a further deeply damaging impact on the local and national economy.

"Both SNP and Labour ministers must pull out all the stops to try and protect these jobs and offer support to those who will be affected."

The Scottish Green Party co-leader, Gillian Mackay, who is also a local MSP, said the move was another "devastating blow" for the area.

"Our governments should be doing more to protect jobs and ensure that workers can benefit from our transition to a greener future," she said.

"Grangemouth is my home, and I am concerned about what this will mean for the local community if it goes ahead."

articles.title: Trump says 'some' munitions are low as Iran stalemate grinds on
articles.summary: He also said in an interview with Time magazine that it was possible the US could ramp up strikes on Iran after November's elections.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has acknowledged that supplies of some munitions "are a little bit lower" as a result of the Iran war but vowed to replenish them to "levels we've never done before".

A report from the Pentagon's inspector general published in mid-July found that the war had led to shortfalls in critical munitions and a bottleneck in resupply.

The US president, however, described the inspector's report at the time as "mostly fake news".

In an interview published by Time on Thursday, Trump also said it was possible the US could ramp up strikes on Iran after the midterm elections in November, despite his previous statements that the US had already achieved victory in the war.

Since the conflict with Iran began in late February, US forces have expended vast quantities of both long-range ground attack systems and the air and missile defences used to intercept Iranian attacks.

The Center for Strategic and International Studies, or CSIS, estimated in July that stocks of some interceptors - such as the Patriot missile and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or Thaad - were significantly depleted, in some cases by more than half.

Despite the dire picture of US shortages painted by multiple assessments, Trump insisted in the Time interview that the US was in "great shape" and "stocking up big".

"Some forms of ammunition are a little bit lower than other forms. We have that middle grade and upper middle grade, which is very powerful," he said.

Trump did not offer specifics on which munitions he was referring to, although he did say that US weapons manufacturers were building plants to manufacture Patriots and Thaads "all over the country".

The US president revealed few details about his plans for the future of the conflict with Iran. Over the weekend, Trump said he had rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

"It's just not good enough," Trump told Time of the offer. He added that a resumption of hostilities was "possible" after November's elections, despite the US having done "an incredible job with that."

In early September, Trump had offered a different view , telling reporters he thought the war would "end immediately after the election because they can't hold out any longer" and that he believed Iran was "desperate to try and affect the election".

Recent polling suggests a significant number of Americans blame Trump's policies, including the war, for rising prices domestically.

Only 17% of US adults approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living and only 26% approved of his handling of the broader economy - a new low - in an Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll that was released on Thursday.

Republican campaign strategists are reportedly worried that negative opinions of Trump will hurt their party's chances in next month's elections, in which control of Congress hangs in the balance.

In the Time interview, however, Trump brushed off polls as "fake numbers" and expressed optimism that he could personally propel Republican candidates to victory in key races next month.

"I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to," he said, adding that "if I campaign for people, those people are going to win".

articles.body:
A man accused of the attempted murder of his 83-year-old mother has pleaded not guilty.

Kevin Mauger, of The Bridge, Vale, appeared at the Royal Court earlier, charged with the attempted murder of Janet Mauger on 13 June.

The 49-year-old pleaded not guilty during a plea and directions hearing before Judge Catherine Fooks.

Mauger was remanded in custody and the case was adjourned until 19 November.

articles.title: Flydubai flight incident: Indian pilot stable, co-pilot in custody; Saudi, UAE launch probes - top developments
articles.summary: A Dubai-Tel Aviv flight carrying 174 people was plunged into chaos on Wednesday after the Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain inside the cockpit
articles.body: A Dubai-Tel Aviv flight carrying 174 people was plunged into chaos on Wednesday after the Omani co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain inside the cockpit and attempted to seize control of the aircraft, forcing it into a sharp descent before it was diverted to Saudi Arabia and landed safely.Indian captain Smit Machchhar, despite being seriously injured, managed to unlock the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew to overpower the attacker and help regain control of the Boeing 737.The flight, flydubai FZ1073, was then diverted to Tabuk, where it landed safely with all 174 people on board.Machchhar was later airlifted to Abu Dhabi for specialised treatment and is now out of danger and recovering, according to the Indian Embassy in the UAE.The incident has triggered investigations by Saudi and UAE authorities, with Israeli investigators also involved. The motive behind the attack has not yet been established.Captain Machchhar recovering in UAEIndian Ambassador to the UAE Deepak Mittal visited Machchhar and his family at the hospital on Thursday and said he was reassured by the pilot’s condition.“Captain Machchhar is in good health and recovering well,” the Indian Embassy said in a post on X, adding that it remained in close coordination with local authorities over his medical care and well-being.“Very reassured to meet Capt Smit. Thank the UAE government for their support and medical care being extended,” Mittal said.External affairs ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal also confirmed the ambassador’s visit.Machchhar was initially taken to a hospital in Tabuk after the flight landed in Saudi Arabia and was subsequently airlifted to Abu Dhabi for specialised treatment.The pilot has more than 13 years of commercial aviation experience and around 9,750 flying hours, predominantly on Boeing 737 aircraft. He previously spent 11 years with SpiceJet as a Line Training Captain.Indian and Israeli leaders hail pilot’s actionsMachchhar has received praise from political leaders in India and Israel following the incident.Prime Minister Narendra Modi said the pilot had demonstrated “remarkable patience, presence of mind, and courage” and said his actions helped prevent what he described as a “9/11-style tragedy”.PM Modi also spoke to Machchhar’s parents and wife and enquired about his health.President Droupadi Murmu said Machchhar’s courage and presence of mind helped prevent a major tragedy and save lives, while defence minister Rajnath Singh said the country took “immense pride” in his actions.External affairs minister S Jaishankar, vice-president C P Radhakrishnan and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge were among those who also praised the pilot.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described Machchhar as a “true hero” and said he had saved the lives of 174 people, including Israeli citizens and other nationals.“Despite being stabbed and seriously injured, he fought back, resisted, opened the cockpit door, and enabled passengers and crew to overpower the attacker — preventing a catastrophic mid-air disaster,” Netanyahu said.Israeli President Isaac Herzog also thanked Machchhar and said he would recommend four passengers for the President's Medal for Civilian Bravery for their role in overpowering the attacker.Saudi Arabia, UAE investigate attackSaudi authorities are conducting the preliminary investigation into the Omani co-pilot, according to an Israeli official cited by The Times of Israel. The suspect is expected to be handed over to Emirati authorities after the Saudi inquiry for a secondary investigation, according to the report.The UAE’s ministry of foreign affairs separately said judicial authorities had opened a comprehensive investigation into the incident.UAE attorney-general counsellor Dr Hamad Al Shamsi has directed a specialised Public Prosecution team to determine the causes and motives behind the incident, the ministry said.The UAE said its judicial authorities have jurisdiction because the aircraft is registered in the country and operates under its national flag.UAE law therefore applies to offences committed aboard the aircraft even when it is outside UAE airspace, it said.The UAE also thanked Saudi authorities for their cooperation in safely landing the aircraft and securing those on board.Motive remains under investigationAccording to Reuters, no motive had yet been determined and an initial Israeli assessment suggested the co-pilot may have acted alone.Two Israeli security officials told Reuters that the investigation remained ongoing. Israel’s envoy to the UAE, Yossi Shelley, also said it was too early to draw conclusions.Israeli intelligence agencies Mossad and Shin Bet are investigating the incident, while Israeli investigators are expected to participate in the interrogation of the suspect.Netanyahu has claimed that the co-pilot underwent “Islamist radical indoctrination” and may have intended to crash the aircraft. He also said investigators would examine whether there was an Iranian connection.However, there had been no official suggestion of Iranian involvement and Israeli security officials had not identified any Iranian role so far.“All possible scenarios, from terrorism to mental disorders, are being looked into. Nothing is ruled out for now,” a regional official briefed on the investigation told news agency AP, speaking on condition of anonymity.The co-pilot has not been publicly identified.Passengers helped overpower attackerThe flight transmitted emergency signals on Wednesday and underwent a sharp descent of more than 17,000 feet from around 34,000 feet before diverting to Tabuk.Passengers who intervened have described how Machchhar opened the cockpit door despite his injuries, allowing them to enter and overpower the co-pilot.Asaf Rajuan, one of the passengers who intervened, described the experience as an instinctive fight for survival.“We felt helpless, suspended in midair, and I didn't know who to turn to. But it was all instinct to survive,” he said in a statement shared by the Israeli presidency.Israeli passenger Yaniv Hayun also described taking control of the aircraft after the attacker was pulled from the cockpit.“We pulled the assailant out, I pulled him out. After I pulled him out we took control of the plane, I pulled up the yoke (steering control of the plane), I straightened the plane out a bit,” he told reporters.The flight was carrying 174 passengers, including 27 children. articles.title: Educating Cardiff teacher admits sexually assaulting teenage girl
articles.summary: Gareth Ritter, who featured in the Channel 4 series, pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl.
articles.body:
A teacher who featured in the Channel 4 documentary series Educating Cardiff has pleaded guilty to sexually assaulting a 17-year-old girl.

Gareth Ritter, 44, of Bryngwyn, in Monmouthshire, was in the middle of giving evidence in his defence when his barrister asked for the charge to be put to him again.

Ritter, who was also a prominent member of a number of brass bands, was asked to stand up and, when asked how he pleaded, he said "guilty".

He was told all of the charges he had admitted carried a custodial sentence and the court would consider immediate custody.

Ritter had previously denied intentionally touching the teenager sexually without consent when he was in his 30s.

Earlier in the trial, the jury was told that, following an event in Cardiff, Ritter offered to drive the victim home but stopped at a flat he owned in Cardiff Bay, saying he had to check it before a new tenant arrived and invited her in.

Once inside, she said he touched her bottom while they stood on a balcony overlooking the city and later kissed her in the hallway.

The woman, now in her 20s, said: "One hand went around my back, it dropped to my bum and he lent in and kissed me.

"I remember his tongue going into my mouth.

"I remember being against the wall, I couldn't step back, I remember him kissing me. I turned my face away, my hands were on him, I wasn't forceful, I held out my hands on his chest. It was a light push but not forceful."

Asked by prosecutor Andrew Davies if she said anything to him, she replied: "It might seem like a strange comment, but I said 'I'm a good girl, I don't do this. I go to a Christian school'."

The court was told Ritter then drove her home, repeatedly asking her if she was going to tell anyone about what had happened.

"I remember him saying 'Nobody needs to know about this. Are you going to tell anyone about this?'

"What do you say in that situation? Gareth was someone I really looked up to. How do you confront that? I'd never been in that situation."

She said she just wanted to "brush it under the carpet".

The court heard the woman reported the alleged incident several years later after Ritter's phone was examined by detectives following an "unrelated matter" that ended with no charges being brought.

Police had found intimate images of a young woman who was under the age of 18. When she was traced, it was the same woman who was sexually assaulted by Ritter.

The court was told the images had originally been screen grabbed with her consent during an intimate video conversation between the woman and another man.

The images had been stored on his tablet, which had been accessed and shared by the man's housemates, and were later found on Ritter's phone.

The jury were told Ritter had since pleaded guilty to the possession and distribution of unlawful images, as the woman was 17 at the time the images were taken.

The woman said when she was told her images had been found on Ritter's phone she decided to report the incident in Cardiff Bay.

The court was told that when Ritter was interviewed by police in December 2022 he denied knowing about the Cardiff Bay flat, and denied taking the woman there. He also told police he had not given her a lift home.

A year later he was interviewed by police again. When asked if he had given a truthful account in his first interview, he said no.

Ritter was granted bail until sentencing on 4 November.

articles.summary: Counter Terrorism police also questioned a UK national, days after five others were arrested and released on bail.
articles.body:
A British-Iranian man has been arrested in connection with an alleged security incident at an airbase in southwest England over the weekend.

Counter Terrorism police in the UK said on Thursday that a “27-year-old man, a dual UK/Iranian national, was arrested” in central London.

He was detained “on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts” as part of an investigation into the events on Sunday near the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford.

A second man, 26 – a UK national – was also “questioned under caution”, the police statement added.

The RAF base 160 kilometres (100 miles) west of London has been used by US bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East, including the US and Israel’s war on Iran, which began in February.

On Sunday, five men, all in their 20s and from London, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and “terrorism” over the incident at RAF Fairford. They have since been released on bail.

“The investigation into circumstances surrounding events in Gloucestershire is hugely complex, and our specialist teams are interrogating multiple lines of enquiry,” Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing for the Metropolitan Police, said in a statement.

“As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.”

Police on Tuesday said they had found no explosives in the vehicles that were parked near the base on Sunday, but had retrieved a “quantity of petrol”.

Earlier, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were “ strong indications ” that Iran played a role in an alleged security incident.

Iran, however, strongly denied any involvement in the incident and the country’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, hit back at Burnham’s allegations, saying British authorities were “barking up the wrong tree”.

Iran’s embassy in London on Monday said the attempts to link Iran to the individuals arrested near the airbase were “fabricated speculations” that fuel “Iranophobia propaganda”.

Al Jazeera’s Rory Challands, reporting from London, said Thursday’s development marked the “sixth arrest” related to the incident, but apart from the nationality of the suspect, “until now nothing in this case has been made public that specifically links Iran to the incident”.

There continues to be lack of clarity around what happened on Sunday, Challands added.

“Much of this whole incident is shrouded in mystery, still. The nature of the threat has still not been officially explained by the British police. There have been no charges in this case so far. The counter-terror police have gone so far only to say that this case is hugely complex … [and that] multiple lines of inquiry are being pursued.”

Since March, the US has used the RAF Fairford airbase to launch attacks on Iran, and the UK has authorised US bombers based there to strike Iranian missile sites targeting ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), a powerful military force that operates alongside the country’s regular armed forces, warned in July that bases used to launch attacks on Iran could be treated as legitimate targets.

articles.title: Immigration experts concerned over delays in H-1B extension for Microsoft, Cognizant, Infosys: 'There has been no clarification'
articles.summary: Immigration attorneys Rahul Reddy and Emily Neumann expressed concern over some tech companies experiencing difficulties in getting H-1B extensions for
articles.body: Immigration attorneys Rahul Reddy and Emily Neumann expressed concern over some tech companies experiencing difficulties in getting H-1B extensions for their employees. Reddy said it is concerning as companies like Microsoft, Cognizant and Infosys employ a huge number of Indians, while Neumann pointed out that there has been no clarification or statement from the departments on this either. The USCIS is reportedly not honoring the premium processing timeline, the attorneys said in their latest weekly discussion.H-1 B extension and premium processingThe H-1B employer files Form I-129, Petition for a Nonimmigrant Worker, requesting an extension of the worker's H-1B status. USCIS specifically requires the petitioner to request an extension on the worker's behalf. The employer can file Form I-907, Request for Premium Processing Service, either together with the I-129 or after the I-129 has already been filed. The beneficiary cannot independently file the I-907 for an ordinary employer-sponsored H-1B; the petitioner or its authorized attorney files it.For an H-1B I-129, premium processing currently requires USCIS to take one of several actions within 15 business days after properly receiving the premium-processing request and fee. That action can be: approval, denial, request for evidence, notice of intent to deny, or opening an investigation for fraud.The H-1B worker does not need to leave the US when the H-1B extension approval is pending. They can work for 240 days while the extension is pending. But after 240 days, the H-1B worker can't work, though they don't have to leave the US.Recently, the Department of Labor suspended new Green Card PERM filings for Cognizant because of a federal fraud investigation but it has nothing to do with H-1B extension cases.On September 18, the Donald Trump administration brought out a new rule where H-1B sponsoring employers will be scanned for their layoff history and if it's found that they fired Americans to hire foreigners, their H-1B petitions won't be entertained. But it is not confirmed whether the H-1B extension delay is a result of this scrutiny.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Israel’s Supreme Court advises Arab party leader to drop election bid
articles.summary: Central Elections Committee voted last week to bar both main Arab lists and two candidates from parliamentary election.
articles.body:
Israel’s Supreme Court has advised Balad party leader Sami Abu Shehadeh to withdraw from the October 27 Knesset election, warning that it could otherwise issue a ruling disqualifying him.

The development came as the court on Thursday began hearing appeals against decisions by Israel’s Central Elections Committee to disqualify Arab electoral lists and candidates from the parliamentary election.

Last week, the elections committee voted to disqualify the country’s two main Arab-majority political lists – Ra’am and the Joint List, which is an alliance of Hadash, Ta’al and Balad. Separately, it moved to disqualify Abu Shehadeh and parliament member Ofer Cassif, a Jewish politician from the Arab-Jewish Hadash party.

Abu Shehadeh is a historian from Jaffa who served in the Knesset on the Joint List from September 2019 until November 2022; Balad was voted out of the Knesset in 2022. Hadash legislator Cassif first appeared on the joint Hadash-Ta’al list in April 2019, in the slot reserved for a Jewish candidate.

On Thursday, the panel of nine justices heard arguments from Abu Shehadeh and his legal team, headed by Hassan Jabareen, according to the Israeli Public Broadcasting Corporation.

Supreme Court President Yitzhak Amit told Abu Shehadeh that a majority of the judges favoured disqualifying his candidacy and gave him until Friday to withdraw, according to the broadcaster. If he does not withdraw, the judges would have to issue a ruling disqualifying his candidacy, according to the report.

National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, whose Otzma Yehudit party petitioned to disqualify Abu Shehadeh, appeared in court wearing a lawyer’s robe. “Sami Abu Shehadeh cannot be a member of Knesset. A supporter of terrorism belongs in prison, not in the Knesset,” he said.

Abu Shehadeh was accused of sympathising with Hamas and of failing to condemn the October 7, 2023 attacks. He denied this at the hearing, saying his words “may have been taken out of context” and that he is “completely opposed to acts of violence”.

Attorney General Gali Baharav-Miara backed his disqualification over an article he published a day after October 7, which she said expressed support for armed struggle. She opposed disqualifying Cassif and the Joint List, saying the evidence did not meet the stringent legal threshold.

Mairav Zonszein, a senior Israel analyst with the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that the banning of Ra’am was particularly “striking”.

“The banning of the Joint List and Balad has almost become a tradition in Israeli politics. However … Ra’am have been part of past coalitions and that its leader, Mansour Abbas, was [a minister without portfolio] in the Bennett-Lapid government. Additionally, it also now has [Yoav Segalovitz] a former police official and a Jewish Israeli politician in its ranks, which makes the attempt more remarkable,” she said.

Israeli affairs expert Shadi al-Sharafa told Al Jazeera that this is “a dangerous precedent that did not exist before”, saying it is the first call to disqualify all Arab representation rather than a single candidate or list.

Al-Sharafa said Arab votes could be decisive in a society “sharply divided between the camp that supports Netanyahu and the camp that opposes him”, and that the petitioners want Abu Shehadeh not only barred from the Knesset, but also put on trial.

The move to ban major Arab parties leaves Palestinian citizens of Israel without major Knesset representation options.

Walid al-Omari, Al Jazeera Arabic’s bureau chief in Ramallah, said that if the court upholds the disqualifications, approximately 20 percent of Arab citizens could be left without representation in the next Knesset.

Israel’s Central Elections Committee is primarily a political body composed of representatives of parliamentary blocs in the outgoing Knesset. In the past, the Supreme Court overturned decisions by the Central Elections Committee to disqualify Arab lists and lawmakers.

articles.title: The 4 best things to buy, and 7 to skip, during October Prime Day — plus, experts share their savings secrets
articles.summary: Before Prime Big Deal Days starts on October 6, shopping experts are breaking down what to buy vs. skip. Plus, learn strategies to save the most money.
articles.body: Once upon a time, October was a quiet month for shopping as we counted down to Black Friday -– but not anymore. Over the past few years, Amazon’s Prime Big Deal Days sale, which is coming up on October 6 and 7, has cemented itself in the retail calendar. And while it’s not necessarily challenging to navigate, I’ve picked up some tips and tricks while covering it that may improve your shopping experience — and, even better, help you save more money. Below, I’m breaking down everything Prime members need to know about what deals are actually worth it, what’s skippable and tips to elevate your savings strategy. I also consulted experts about what you need to know, like the major differences between October Prime Day and Black Friday. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What to buy during October Prime Day Household basics and groceries Think about the most boring things on your shopping list: paper towels, protein powder, moisturizer, dog treats, socks and laundry detergent, for example. Those are some of the best products to buy during Prime Big Deal Days. Brands know shoppers are increasingly concerned about rising prices, especially leading up to the holidays, so they’re dropping prices on essentials you can’t avoid buying. “Everyday costs are putting pressure on household budgets, and October Prime Day can be an opportunity to take some of that pressure off by stocking up on the non-perishable things your household goes through anyway,” says Stephanie Carls, a retail insights expert at RetailMeNot, an online coupon and savings platform. “A discount on something already on your list can help free up money in your budget for other holiday expenses.” I say it every Prime Day: My number one piece of advice is to walk around your home and make a list of your repeat buys. Add those to your cart first during the sale, and use whatever’s left in your budget to get less necessary items. That’s not to say you should ignore deals from other tech brands. Apple, Sonos, Beats, Anker, Bose, Sony and more also drop prices on earbuds, Bluetooth speakers, smart home devices, portable chargers and smartwatches. But Amazon-owned devices are historically the most competitive since Amazon is the retailer hosting the sale and the brand selling the product, says Carls. It’s also the last major sale before Halloween and Thanksgiving, so brands discount hosting supplies and festive decor, as well as cozy apparel and footwear. Buying these types of products now lets you use them for the next few weeks. Holiday gifts are also top of mind for shoppers during Prime Big Deal Days, but only certain ones are worth getting. If your loved ones have beauty products, gadgets and small home and kitchen appliances on their wish lists, now is the time to buy. Wait on most toys and gaming consoles, however — shop during Black Friday and Cyber Monday instead. Coffee makers, vacuums, toaster ovens, air purifiers and more go on sale throughout the event, and some of them even hit their lowest prices ever. That’s when you’ll see a bigger selection of discounted items and lower overall prices. ToysTVsLaptopsVideo game consolesMajor home and kitchen appliancesFurnitureMattresses Are October Prime Day deals worse this year? No, October Prime Day deals aren’t worse this year due to the current economic climate, according to the experts I talked to. In fact, because Amazon, Target and Walmart, three of the nation’s biggest retailers, are hosting their mega sales during the same week, they’re competing for your cart, which could motivate them to drop prices a little more than they originally planned to win you over, says Carls. That said, high inflation rates, the skyrocketing cost of fuel and looming changes in tariff policies may cause brands to raise baseline prices and offer weaker discounts in the future. If you find a worthwhile deal on something you really need during October sales, don’t wait to buy it, says Porwal — that might cause you to pay more down the line. How to save the most money during October Prime Day Plan ahead October Prime Day runs on urgency. Limited-time deals sell out quickly, so planning is crucial. Before you start adding products to your cart, I recommend doing the following: Make a shopping list: It helps you monitor prices on the products you actually need and avoid getting distracted by other things you aren’t planning on buying, says Carls. I recommend making a shopping list by adding items to Your Lists on Amazon’s website and/or app so everything is in one place.Set up deal alerts: Amazon adds new October Prime Day deals at 12 a.m., 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. PT each day of the event. Instead of wasting time browsing, ask Alexa for Shopping, Amazon’s AI shopping assistant, to alert you when specific products, brands and products you frequently buy in general categories drop in price. Plus, there might be restocks if something sells out. Alexa for Shopping can help you shop Prime Big Deal Days in other ways, too — learn more here. Track prices and comparison shop Tracking prices is one of the only ways to know whether an October Prime Day deal is actually a good one. Evaluate price history graphs closely, which are available on some Amazon product pages and sites like CamelCamelCamel. They tell you whether the deal price is truly the lowest a product has dropped to in a while, or if it’s marked down from an inflated baseline. At NBC Selected, we don’t consider an October Prime Day deal “good” unless it’s at its lowest price in at least three months and recently dropped in price. Comparison shopping is important, too, says Vipin Porwal, the founder of and a consumer expert at Smarty, an online shopping rewards app.. Other big retailers are hosting sales within the next week that overlap with Prime Big Deal Days, so before you checkout, make sure items aren’t available elsewhere for a lower price. Compare shipping fees and how much cashback you can potentially earn, too. Shop Lightning Deals Lightning Deals drop as often as every 10 minutes and only run for a few hours. There’s also limited inventory available — once the product sells out or the deal expires, it’s gone for good. Lightning Deals are some of the most lucrative discounts brands offer during Prime Big Deal Days, so pay close attention to them, says Porwal. NBC Select also tracks them live to help you stay updated. Additionally, Porwal recommends taking note of the main deals Amazon advertises on its website’s and app’s homepage and landing pages. They tend to get the most visible placement because they’re some of the best savings opportunities. Stack savings Amazon typically doesn’t offer promo codes that you can stack on top of deals, but sometimes you’ll find “coupons” you can clip on certain product pages, which take a few additional dollars off the discounted item, says Carls. Also try to pay with a credit card that lets you earn points, rewards or cash back as you spend on Amazon. Familiarize yourself with return policies Amazon doesn’t have a special return policy for Prime Day purchases, but you should know how long you have to return an item if needed. Learn more here. articles.title: Phil Mickelson sought treatment for addiction and family trauma, spokesperson says
articles.summary: Golf legend Phil Mickelson checked himself into a treatment facility earlier this year to address family trauma and addiction, his spokesperson confirmed to NBC News Thursday.
articles.body: Golf legend Phil Mickelson checked himself into a treatment facility earlier this year to address family trauma and addiction, his spokesperson confirmed to NBC News Thursday. Mickelson, 56, is no longer at the facility, and it is not clear when he entered treatment or for how long. His representative did not give further details about the nature of his stay at the unnamed facility and declined to answer additional questions. The announcement comes amid a turbulent year for the six-time major champion. In April, Mickelson said he would step away from competition for an extended period while his family navigated “a personal health matter.” Mickelson, who is married and has three children, was reportedly barred from his longtime Southern California golf club, The Farms Golf Club, after being accused of making “nonconsensual and inappropriate physical contact” with a female club employee. The allegations were first reported by Golf Digest, citing multiple sources. At the time, a representative for Mickelson described the encounter as a “misunderstanding.” Mickelson’s attorney, Tom Locke, said in a statement: “There is a great deal of misinformation circulating and, while Phil’s full attention is devoted to a private family health matter, he has retained defamation counsel and is determined to hold accountable any publication or individual trafficking in speculation or false rumors.” Mickelson is far from the first professional athlete to seek treatment for addiction. Olympic champion Michael Phelps went to rehab in 2014 after a DUI arrest. This spring, golf champion Tiger Woods said he was seeking treatment for substance abuse after his vehicle rolled over in Florida and he was charged with driving under the influence in March. Mickelson has won 45 PGA Tour events, including six majors.

articles.title: Cornel West and Sean Hannity find unlikely common ground despite deep political divide
articles.summary: Cornel West and Sean Hannity clash over socialism, Iran and immigration but reveal a surprising personal bond on "Hang Out with Sean Hannity."
articles.body: Cornel West says he doesn't live to meet others' expectations, a philosophy he displayed by sitting down with Fox News host Sean Hannity despite their deep political differences. "People say, ‘How could you even sit with Brother Sean? Why could you call Sean a brother?’" West said during Thursday's episode of "Hang Out with Sean Hannity." "I don't live my life in order to satisfy other people's expectations." The progressive scholar sparred with Hannity over socialism, Iran, immigration and President Donald Trump, but the conversation also revealed a personal connection between the two men. JD VANCE DEFENDS 'THE VIEW' APPEARANCE, EXPLAINS THE NEED TO ENGAGE WITH HOSTILE ENVIRONMENTS West repeatedly referred to Hannity as "Brother Sean," explaining that his Christian faith compels him to see every person as a fellow human being regardless of ideology. "Each person is a brother and a sister, no matter what their politics are, what ideology, what color, their gender, their sexual orientation. They're human beings at that deepest level," he said. "So when I see you, I see Brother Sean." Hannity acknowledged that he expected the conversation to be more combative, saying despite their differences, "I just can't help but like you." The two men disagreed over an array of issues while maintaining civility. During a discussion about the war with Iran, West accused the U.S. of committing a war crime by killing Iranian civilians. TRUMP IS DISMANTLING IRAN’S WAR MACHINE, BUT AMERICA STILL NEEDS AN ENDGAME "The precious children who were killed by U.S. bombs, that was wrong," West said. "That's a war crime." Hannity pushed back against West's characterization, arguing that Iran's support for terrorism and attacks that killed Americans made the country responsible for the war. Hannity also cited the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, arguing that they prevented further American casualties. The wide-ranging conversation also touched on education, poverty and the role of government, with West arguing that public institutions must do more to protect poor and working-class Americans, an argument Hannity disputed. articles.title: US agency sues Harvard over hiring records in probe into alleged discrimination against white men
articles.summary: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has sued Harvard University seeking records related to an investigation into whether the Ivy League
articles.body: The US Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) has sued Harvard University seeking records related to an investigation into whether the Ivy League school discriminated against white men and other groups in its hiring practices.The lawsuit, filed in a federal court in Boston late Tuesday, seeks to force Harvard to comply with an EEOC subpoena for documents and data related to faculty recruitment since 2018. The agency is investigating whether the university violated Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits employment discrimination based on race and sex, Reuters reported.The case stems from a civil rights charge filed in April 2025 by EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, a Trump appointee. Lucas alleged that Harvard had engaged in systemic discrimination against white, Asian, male and heterosexual employees and job applicants as part of efforts to diversify its faculty.According to the charge, Harvard adopted programmes that contributed to an increase in faculty employment across demographic groups since 2013, except among white men.Lucas cited data previously published on Harvard's website showing that the share of white men among tenured faculty fell from 64% in 2013 to 56% in 2023.The EEOC said Harvard had provided some records but resisted handing over a broader set of documents, including information on all applicants for faculty positions since 2018. The agency has asked a judge to order the university to comply with its subpoena.Harvard has denied discriminating on the basis of race or sex and said it hires and promotes faculty based on merit, qualifications and individual accomplishments.A university spokesperson said Harvard had been responding to the EEOC's inquiries in good faith and would continue defending itself against what it called "illegal government overreach."Harvard's lawyers have also argued that the EEOC investigation is part of the Trump administration's broader campaign against the university and that the government is retaliating against Harvard for challenging its demands.The lawsuit is the latest legal clash between Harvard and the Trump administration. The university has previously secured court rulings blocking government efforts to cut more than USD 2 billion in federal research funding and prevent it from hosting international students.The EEOC under Lucas has stepped up scrutiny of diversity, equity and inclusion programmes at companies and educational institutions. The agency has also pursued discrimination-related investigations involving several major institutions.Separately, the US Department of Justice is seeking records from Harvard as part of an investigation into whether the university considers race in its student admissions process.You use AI every day. articles.title: Diddy placed in solitary following NBC News report on his VIP prison life
articles.summary: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison.
articles.body: Sean “Diddy” Combs has been placed in solitary confinement following an NBC News report on his VIP lifestyle inside prison, according to a source with knowledge of the matter. The disgraced hip hop mogul arrived at the Fort Dix federal prison in New Jersey in October after he was sentenced to 50 months behind bars for transporting people across state lines for sexual encounters. Since then, he has spent thousands of dollars a month to bring his high-end lifestyle to the low-security prison, NBC News reported Tuesday in a story based on interviews with four men who spent time in the same unit as Combs. They said he had no trouble acquiring contraband items such as cellphones and premium liquor, including Hennessy. He also pays several inmates who cook special meals for him, clean the toilet and shower areas before he uses them, do his laundry, make his bed and even give him Chinese-style massages. “This is not some normal s--- you see in jail. This is some rich s---,” one of the sources said. “It looks crazy, but again, it’s Diddy.” NBC News also obtained photos and videos inside the prison, which includes footage of Combs appearing to use a contraband cellphone. After the report was published, Combs was removed from his dormitory-style quarters and placed in a special housing unit, better known as solitary confinement or the SHU, according to the source. A Bureau of Prisons spokesperson would neither confirm nor deny that Combs was moved. “For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or whether a particular individual is the subject of allegations, investigations, or sanctions,” the spokesperson said. TMZ was first to report that the Bad Boy Records founder was moved to solitary. Federal prisons often transfer inmates to the special housing unit when they are the subjects of an investigation, experts say. “We’d put people in the SHU while we were gathering evidence,” said Vito Maraviglia, a retired special investigator for the Bureau of Prisons who worked at Fort Dix in the late 1990s. Maraviglia said the New Jersey prison is known as one of the cushiest in the federal prison system. It has segmented housing areas that are more difficult to monitor than at other facilities, making it easier for inmates to hide and use contraband items like cellphones. “A high-profile guy like that, with all that money, I’m surprised they put him at a place like Fort Dix,” Maraviglia said. Inmates placed in the SHU are locked in a cell with one other person for at least 23 hours a day, according to two men who spent time at Fort Dix. Inmates are allowed a book or two and a wind-up radio, the sources said, and they must wear an orange jumpsuit instead of the regular khaki uniform or grey sweatpants and shirts. Meals are delivered in trays but commissary access is restricted, and they are permitted to shower only a few days a week. The sources said they must otherwise wash up in a sink. “It’s nasty down there,” one of the sources said. It isn’t Combs’ first time in solitary confinement at Fort Dix. Last summer, he was placed in the special housing unit after he got into a fight with another inmate. He was later kicked out of a drug treatment program at the prison but continued paying inmates to do a range of services for him, NBC News reported Tuesday. The story prompted responses from people as varied as Combs’ longtime nemesis 50 Cent and the prominent attorney Gloria Allred, who represents a woman suing him for allegedly raping her more than 20 years ago. (Combs has denied the allegations, and the case is ongoing.) “These serious allegations against Mr. Combs cry out for an immediate federal investigation and appropriate federal action including a prosecution if the allegations of having and using a cell phone while incarcerated can be proven beyond a reasonable doubt,” Allred said in a statement. Other famous people have also received perks in prison, including Martha Stewart and Harvey Weinstein. Combs’ trial last year centered on drug-fueled orgies he organized called “freak offs.” They involved male sex workers and his former girlfriends – including the singer Cassie – who filed a lawsuit against Combs alleging years of physical and sexual abuse. (The case was settled, with Combs denying any wrongdoing.) The trial ended in a split verdict, with a New York jury finding him not guilty on the more serious charges of sex trafficking and racketeering charges that could have put him in prison for life.

articles.title: Father hoped NYT executive son would visit home weeks before prosecutors allege deadly in-law ambush
articles.summary: A father's loving Facebook post surfaced days before New York Times executive Jonathan McKinsey was allegedly ambushed in a California park.
articles.body: A Facebook message from a father urging his son to come home surfaced days after a New York Times executive was allegedly gunned down by his 77-year-old in-laws in a California park. The executive, Jonathan McKinsey, shared a smiling photo of himself on Facebook Sept. 7. His father, William Finney II, commented beneath the post with a message expressing hope the family could reunite. "Jon, hope everything is going well," Finney wrote. "Hope you can visit us when you have some free time. Mom and Dad love you so much and miss you. Hope everything goes well with you and Candice and the kids." LAW PROFESSOR'S KILLER STALKED HIM 'LIKE A SHARK CIRCLING' BEFORE EX-MOTHER-IN-LAW'S MURDER-FOR-HIRE AMBUSH Less than three weeks later, McKinsey, 40, was fatally shot in the parking lot of the Dublin Sports Grounds, where prosecutors allege his in-laws, Shouyong Zhang and Shili Chen, both 77, carried out a planned ambush. The Alameda County District Attorney's Office charged the couple with murder and accused them of intentionally killing McKinsey by "lying in wait." SUSPECT IN MICROSOFT EXECUTIVE JARED BRIDEGAN'S MURDER CONVICTED IN ROADSIDE AMBUSH Several 911 callers reported gunfire before a Dublin Police Services sergeant arrived and found McKinsey with multiple gunshot wounds. Witnesses pointed officers toward a black Honda Civic leaving the parking lot, leading police to conduct a high-risk traffic stop nearby, according to court documents. Chen was allegedly driving while Zhang sat in the passenger seat. OHIO MAN CONVICTED AFTER TRYING TO SHOOT EX-WIFE AT POINT-BLANK RANGE INSIDE RESTAURANT IN CHILLING VIDEO Three witnesses identified Chen and Zhang as the shooters, while surveillance video allegedly captured the couple opening fire "in concert" on McKinsey. Police allege the couple opened fire in a crowded parking lot with "blatant disregard for public safety," even as several children were nearby. articles.title: Amber Guyger, ex-Dallas police officer, granted parole after Botham Jean murder conviction
articles.summary: Former Dallas police officer Amber Guyger was granted parole just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering neighbor Botham Jean in a 2018 shooting.
articles.body: A former Dallas police officer was granted parole on Thursday just under seven years after she was convicted of murdering her neighbor in a 2018 shooting. Amber Guyger, 38, was granted parole by the Texas Board of Pardons and Paroles, the board said in a statement. In 2019, Guyger was convicted of murdering 26-year-old Black man Botham Jean. Guyger told authorities that she shot Jean after mistakenly walking into his apartment, believing it to be her own, according to officials. She told authorities she believed Jean was an intruder. Jean was eating ice cream in his living room and not armed, according to authorities. The former police officer was sentenced to 10 years in prison for the crime. Prosecutors asked jurors to sentence Guyger to at least 28 years. The Texas board said that Guyger was granted parole because she did not have a documented pattern of violent arrests, she “maintained a satisfactory institutional adjustment” and completed programs “that should enhance chances to obtain and maintain full-time stable employment” during her imprisonment. Guyger initially became eligible for parole on September 29, 2024. Her initial review occurred on October 10, 2024, and resulted in a parole denial with her next review being scheduled on or about October 2026. During her trial, questions were raised about the role race may have played in the killing. Prosecutors revealed racist text messages the former police officer sent, unrelated to Jean or his killing. One of the texts was about the Martin Luther King Jr. parade in Dallas in 2018. “When does this end lol,” an officer wrote to Guyger. “When MLK is dead … oh wait …,” she joked. Two days before Guyger killed Jean, she texted someone who had just adopted a German Shepherd. The dog’s owner wrote that the dog “may be racist.” Guyger replied: “It’s okay ... I’m the same.” Prosecutors said that Jean was watching television and eating a bowl of vanilla ice cream in his living room just before 10 p.m. when Guyger burst inside and shot him. Guyger testified that she used her electronic key fob to open Jean’s door and that she immediately drew her service weapon once she was inside. The prosecution said the trajectory of the bullet showed that Jean was either getting up from his couch or cowering when Guyger fired at him. A lawyer for Jean’s family, Lee Merritt, said in a statement to NBC News Dallas-Fort Worth that the family was “disappointed by the decision.” “A 10-year sentence was already a fraction of what was lost,” Merritt said. “Releasing Ms. Guyger after seven years makes that loss feel even smaller in the eyes of the system. It is not. The family still lives with this loss every day.” Jean’s family said in a statement on Thursday that they are requesting privacy at this time. “To all of the many well-wishers who have continued to say Botham’s name and carry his memory, they wish to give their thanks for the continuing support,” the family said in a statement. Jean’s brother, Brandt Jean, said he forgave Guyger during her sentencing in 2019. “I personally want the best for you,” he said at the time. “I wasn’t even going to say this before my family, but I don’t even want you to go to jail. I want the best for you, because I know that’s exactly what Botham would want you to do — to give your life to Christ.” The Dallas Police Department said in a statement that it had “no role in this decision.” “The Dallas Police Department understands this decision may bring renewed attention and emotion surrounding the tragic death of Botham Jean,” the department said. “Our thoughts remain with the Jean family and all those impacted by his loss.” Jean grew up in Saint Lucia before coming to the United States to go to Harding University in Arkansas, which he graduated from in 2016. He was working as an accountant for one of the most prestigious accounting firms in the world, PricewaterhouseCoopers, in Dallas when he was killed. He would have turned 35-years-old on Tuesday.

articles.title: After Red Sea losses, Yemen’s government forces hold the line
articles.summary: Air strikes and difficult terrain have prevented the Houthis from turning coastal gains into a wider breakthrough.
articles.body:
Yemen’s Houthi rebels conducted intense attacks across frontlines in Taiz governorate on Thursday, as the Iran-allied group attempts to build on its lighting offensive that captured the country’s Red Sea coast last month.

Thus far, Yemeni government forces have been able to hold their positions on the frontlines and even claimed to have inflicted heavy losses against the Houthis.

Still, there are few signs that the Saudi-backed government intends to begin a serious counteroffensive against the Houthis in the near future, despite the head of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council Rashad al-Alimi calling for a general mobilisation against the rebels on September 25.

The government instead seems to be pursuing a more gradual process, building up its military forces and attempting to make them more cohesive.

Abdul Basir al-Bahr, a senior official with the internationally recognised government army’s Taiz Military Axis, told Al Jazeera that the general mobilisation call was part of that effort.

Al-Bahr said plans include bringing reserve personnel back into the military’s ranks and retraining them, alongside local anti-Houthi fighters and civilian volunteers.

He stressed that the measures were at an early stage and their battlefield impact could not be judged yet.

In Taiz, Al Jazeera’s field monitoring has found that fighting has continued since early September without any major shifts that can be directly attributed to the general mobilisation.

The picture is similar on other fronts, including the Kahboub Mountains overlooking the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and in Lahj, south of Taiz.

Yemeni government field commanders told Al Jazeera the general mobilisation had not yet led to frontline reinforcements.

But that does not mean that military activity has not intensified. On Monday, Colonel Majid al-Nazili, spokesman for the government’s military forces, said the forces had carried out more than 400 strikes over a 24-hour period against the Houthis, causing losses in personnel and equipment.

The ability of the Yemeni government’s military to halt further Houthi advances since the Red Sea reversal appears to reflect a combination of more favourable defensive terrain in the Taiz mountains and Lahj, as well as increased firepower.

The loss of the coastline was aided by weak coordination among anti-Houthi forces, who – despite officially being under one military chain of command – appeared divided and unable to respond quickly to the Houthi advance.

In both Taiz and Lahj – as well as Marib in Yemen’s north – anti-Houthi forces have shown more unity and have years of experience preventing Houthi military advances. Government-aligned forces have also had time to reinforce areas where the Houthis are attempting to advance.

The use of air power is also growing, with government forces reporting hundreds of air, drone, artillery and other strikes targeting Houthi positions and reinforcements in the past few days.

After having seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, the Houthis now need control of the mountainous high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and the roads leading inland to consolidate those gains. Their attempts to take that high ground have so far failed, while the expanded territory has increased the manpower and logistical burden of defending their new positions.

The result, so far, is increasingly a battle over roads and supply lines, with neither side so far able to reproduce the kind of rapid breakthrough seen on the Red Sea coast.
